Office of the Secretary 

 Regu lations, Title 15, Subtitle A; Title 44, Chapter VIII] The Secretary 

The Secretary is responsible for the administration of the functions and authorities assigned to the Department of Commerce by law and for advising the President on Federal policy and programs affecting the industrial and commercial segments of the national economy within the scope of the Department.

OFFICE OF PUBLIC INFORMATION.- 

This office, reporting through the 

Special  for

Public Affairs, guides and directs all informational programs within the Department.

OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNSEL.- The General Counsel is the chief law officer of the Department and serves as legal adviser to the Secretarial officers and other officers of the Department. This office is responsible for and supervises all legal activities of the Department and supervises and coordinates the development of the Department's legislative program. 

OFFICE OF CONGRESSIONAL RELA- TIONS.-The Special Assistant to the Secretary for Congressional Relations advises the Secretary and other officers of the Department on congressional relation. This office provides information to the Congress on the programs of the Department and supervises the handling of congressional correspondence and inquiries. It keeps the Department advised of the progress of the Department's legislative program in the Congress and of other pertinent congressional activity.

SPECIAL ASSISTANT TO THE SECRE- TARY FOR TEXTILE PROGRAMS.-The 

Special Assistant to the Secretary for

Textile Programs has central responsibility for assisting the Secretary in followup of the President's programs for textiles, of enforcement of the regulation of textile imports under international agreements, and of other textile programs. He is chairman of the Inter agency Textile Administrative Com mittee which has responsibility for the implementation of the international agreements.

NATIONAL EXPORT EXPANSION CO- ORDINATOR.-The National Export Ex pansion Coordinator, appointed by the President and stationed in the Department of Commerce, is charged with coordinating all parts of the Ex port Expansion Program. The Coor dinator functions across departmental lines to assure maximum combined impact of all efforts aimed at expansion of exports.

EXECUTIVE SECRETARIAT.-The Ex ecutive Secretariat, which serves in a staff capacity to the Secretary and Under Secretary, provides a central coordinating unit for timely dissemination of valuable information relating to policy matters among top Department officials. This office is also responsible for the coordination and review of all incoming and outgoing communications for the Secretary and Under Secretary, as well as for expediting the flow of internal communications. 

The Under Secretary The Under Secretary of Commerce serves as the principal deputy of the Secretary in all matters affecting the Department of Commerce and exercises general supervision over its several bureaus and offices. He also serves as acting Secretary in the Secretary's absence.

The Under Secretary of Commerce for Transportation 

[For regulations codified under this heading, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 14, Chapter XV; Title 32A, Chapter VII]

The Under Secretary of Commerce for Transportation serves as the Secre tary's principal assistant on transportation policy within the Department and helps to establish and maintain the Department's position with respect to the establishment of an integrated transportation program for the Department and the development of overall transportation policy within the executive branch of the Government, including the mobilization aspects. He has responsibility for coordination of interdepartmental transportation decisionmaking in assigned areas, and responsibility for policy-level research in such areas as Federal investment in transportation, improvements in intermodal and intramodal practices af- =fecting the public interest, and sug- Igestions for additions or changes in 

Federal legislation.

He exercises policy direction and general supervision over the Maritime

Administration and the Bureau of Public Roads. 

OFFICE OF EMERGENCY TRANSPORTA- 

TION. This office is a constituent unit which develops and coordinates overall policies, plans, and procedures for the provision of centralized control of all modes of transportation in an emergency for the movement of passenger and freight traffic of all types and the determination of the proper apportionment and allocation of the total civil transportation capacity or any portion thereof to meet overall essential needs. 

Included within this overall coordinating function is the operational planning responsibility for the development of a national program to utilize the air carrier civil air transportation capacity and equipment, both domestically and internationally, in a national emergency based on requirements from the Department of Defense, Civil Aeronautics Board, and other agencies and the allocation of air carrier aircraft to meet these requirements.

GREAT LAKES PILOTAGE ADMINIS- TRATION. -The Great Lakes Pilotage 

Administration, a constituent unit, ad ministers the Great Lakes Pilotage Act of 1960 which provides for the establishment of an effective system of regulated pilotage on the Great Lakes.

The responsibilities include the registration of United States pilots, the regulation of pilotage pools, and the establishment of rates and charges for pilot age services. The Administration is further authorized to enter into arrangements with Canada for reciprocal pooling, equitable participation by 

United States and Canadian pilots, and the establishment of joint or identical rates and charges. [For regulations codified under Great 

Lakes Pilotage Administration, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 46, Chapter III] The Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Economic Affairs The Assistant Secretary of Com merce for Economic Affairs serves as principal adviser to the Secretary on broad, long-range, economic programs, as well as adviser to other departmental officials with respect to matters of economic policy positions and recommendations. His responsibilities include coordination and review of the economic research and statistical programs in the Department. He serves as the Department's liaison with the Council of Economic Advisers. He also exercises policy direction and general supervision over the Bureau of the 

Census and the Office of Business Economics. 

The Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Domestic and International

Business The Assistant Secretary of Com merce for Domestic and International Business serves as the principal adviser to the Secretary on all domestic and international aspects of the Department's responsibilities concerning industry, trade, investment, and related economic activities. He exercises policy di-

rection over the Bureau of International Commerce, the Business and

Commerce Department participation in trade conferences, national and regional conventions of trade and industry associations, and other meetings in which such participation advances U.S. economic growth. It provides publications and information service for the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Domestic and International Business and the organization units under his office.

The Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Science and Technology The Assistant Secretary of Com merce for Science and Technology serves as adviser to all departmental officials with respect to matters of science and technology and in this capacity has cognizance over the research and development activities carried out in the fields of science and technology by all organization units of the Department. He exercises policy direction and general supervision over the National Bureau of Standards, the Coast and Geodetic Survey, the 

Weather Bureau, and the Patent Office. 

OFFICE OF THE FEDERAL COORDINA- TOR FOR METEOROLOGICAL SERVICES AND SUPPORTING RESEARCH.-This of fice, which is a constituent unit, has the responsibility assigned to the Secretary of Commerce under a Bureau of the Budget directive for coordinating and planning all Federal activities relating to weather services and research designed to improve weather services. 

The primary objective is to achieve effectual and economical weather services which are adequate to meet the needs of the Nation.

The Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Administration The Assistant Secretary of Com merce for Administration is the principal deputy and adviser to the Secretary of Commerce on all matters of administration and management, and is the chief officer of the Department on such matters. OFFICE OF BUDGET AND FINANCE.- 

This office is responsible for the direction and supervision of the financial and budgetary activities of the Department and its constituent units. 

OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE SER- 

VICES. This office is responsible for formulating plans and policies relating to administrative services and facilities operations throughout the Department and for direction and supervision of the activities thereunder.

OFFICE OF PERSONNEL.-This office is responsible for all personnel programing and management activities of the Department including manpower controls, employee utilization, labor re lations, and health.

OFFICE OF PUBLICATIONS.-This of fice directs and coordinates publications development, sales promotion and distribution, and printing activities of the Department. It operates a central printing service for the Department.

OFFICE OF AUDITS.-This office co ordinates the audit activities of the

Department, including developing and prescribing departmental audit policies and guidelines, and executes substantive audits as necessary to provide the Secretary and other officials of the

Department with timely and objective information concerning the operating, administrative, and financial activities of primary organization units. 

OFFICE OF INVESTIGATIONS AND SE- CURITY.-The Director of this office serves as staff adviser to the Assistant Secretary and the several bureaus and offices on all matters pertaining to security within the Department. The office is responsible for developing policies and procedures for physical and personnel security and assuring their application throughout the Department. It is also responsible for the development and application of policies, procedures, and standards for the maintenance of ethical conduct and practices of employees of the Department in the performance of their re spective duties. 

OFFICE OF MANAGEMENT AND ORGA- NIZATION. This office is responsible for organization planning, the improvement of management systems, techniques, and practices, and the development of departmentwide general management policies and improvement programs. 

OFFICE OF EMERGENCY READINESS. 

This office develops and provides for the execution of plans for the continuity of the Department's emergency functions, civil defense program, and natural disaster activities. Through its eight Regional Emergency Planning 

Coordinators, this office assists the States and local governments in the development of plans for the emergency management of production and transportation resources.

U.S. COMMISSION-NEW YORK WORLD'S FAIR.-This office has the responsibility for planning and executing the U.S. Government exhibition at the New York World's Fair, 19641965.

Area Redevelopment Administration 

 Regu lations, Title 13, Chapter III] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Area Redevelopment Administration was established by the Secretary of 

Commerce, by Department Order 171 

of May 8, 1961, pursuant to authority vested in the Secretary of Commerce by the Area Redevelopment Act (75 

Stat. 47; 42 U.S.C. 2501) and Reor ganization Plan 5 of 1950. Following enactment of the Public Works Acceleration Act (76 Stat. 541; 42 U.S.C. 

2641) and the issuance of Executive

Order 11049, Department Order 171 

was amended on September 14, 1962, to establish within the Area Redevelop ment Administration the Office of Public Works Acceleration. 

PURPOSE. The primary function as signed the Area Redevelopment Administration by statute is the economic redevelopment of areas of substantial and persistent unemployment and underemployment through the creation of new employment opportunities by developing new and expanding existing facilities and resources in such areas. 

ORGANIZATION.-The organization of the Area Redevelopment Administra tion comprises the Office of the 

Administrator, the Office of Administration, the Office of Financial As sistance, the Office of Operations, the Office of Planning and Research, and the Office of Public Works Accelera tion, at the Washington, D.C., headquarters. 

In accordance with the terms of the 

Area Redevelopment Act, a National Public Advisory Committee on Area 

Redevelopment serves to promote full exchange of views between the Government and the public, and an Area 

Redevelopment Advisory Policy Board 

(an interagency committee) helps assure coordinated action by Federal

Government agencies on area redevelopment matters. 

Field representatives of the Agency are located throughout the United 

States and Puerto Rico. 

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-The 

Area Redevelopment Act authorizes certain Federal aids for areas designated by the Administrator as "redevelopment areas." These include loans for industrial or commercial facilities, loans and/or grants for public facilities, technical assistance, and related infor mation. The Area Redevelopment Ad ministration exercises program control and provides policy direction in furnishing such aid in close collaboration with other Federal agencies.

The Office of Public Works Accel eration recommends administrative and contingency allocations under the accelerated public works program and prepares reports on this program which, in order to increase employment opportunities, has initiated and/ or accelerated public works in eligible areas throughout the United States. 

The Administration coordinates op erating functions under the Area Redevelopment Act delegated by the 

Secretary of Commerce to the Depart ments of Agriculture, Health, Educa tion, and Welfare, Interior, and Labor, to the Housing and Home Finance Agency, and to the Small Business Ad ministration. These functions include technical assistance and economic de- 2:

انا velopment information as well as the processing of loan and grant applications.

The Administration's staff of field representatives provides direct assistance to State and local agencies concerned with, and engaged in, economic development activities.

Business and Defense Services Administration 

 Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter VI; Title 32A, Chapter VI; Title 44, Chapter IV; Title 48, Chapter III] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.- -The Business and Defense Services Admin istration was established by the Secretary of Commerce on October 1, 1953, by Department Order 152, pursuant to authority of Reorganization Plan 5 of 

1950.

ORGANIZATION.-The Administrator of BDSA is responsible to the Assistant 

Secretary for Domestic and International Business. Programs of BDSA are executed by 26 business and industry divisions, grouped by related industries into seven offices: Marketing and Services, Chemicals and Consumer

Products, Industrial Equipment, Met als and Minerals, Scientific and Tech nical Equipment, Construction and Materials Industries, and Textiles. 

FUNCTIONS.-BDSA is in daily con tact with industry and business to keep informed of significant changes and problems confronting the business community. BDSA is thereby enabled to provide active assistance in seven major program areas that directly involve the industry and commerce of the United States.

INDUSTRIAL MODERNIZATION.- 

BDSA assesses the effect of industrial

change on individual industries. It evaluates the impact of new materials and processes, and the business and economic consequences of changes in industrial practices. BDSA cooperates with industry to broaden awareness of available techniques to increase productivity, employment, and profits through modernization conferences. 

FOREIGN COMMODITY TRADE SUP- 

PORT.-BDSA provides advice and counsel to industries on international business opportunities, tariff questions, commodity problems and market prospects abroad. It contributes to the development of commercial policy by assessing the impact of imports on U.S. industry.

LEGISLATION AND REGULATION. 

Within the Department's legislative program BDSA initiates and supports new legislation designed to expand business opportunities in the United 

States, and reviews and recommends changes in existing regulations to remove burdensome and outdated restrictions on industrial innovation and inventiveness.

GOVERNMENT SERVICE S.- -BDSA 

helps to develop more meaningful and useful business statistics. It advises other agencies on the nature of business operations to assure fully informed decision making. BDSA prepares data necessary for fruitful and mutually beneficial tariff negotiations. 

GOVERNMENT-BUSINESS 

RELA- TIONS.-BDSA assists business to deal effectively with its policy problems involving the Federal Government. It advises Government agencies dealing with business problems about the potential impact of contemplated actions. 

DOMESTIC INDUSTRIAL AND MARKET REPORTING.-BDSA cooperates with business in preparation of special industry studies best performed by a 

Government agency. BDSA works with other Government agencies to collect and distribute business data which industry considers necessary.

INDUSTRIAL MOBILIZATION.-BDSA 

administers the authority delegated to the Secretary of Commerce under the

Defense Production Act of 1950, as amended, with respect to the use of priorities and directives that are necessary to support and expedite the accomplishment of current military, atomic, and space programs through the operation of the Defense Materials 

System. It plans for industrial mobilization and production control in a national emergency, recruits and trains all members of the National Defense Executive Reserve, and provides advice and counsel to the Office of 

Emergency Planning on national stockpile acquisitions, disposals, and specifications.

TRADE ADJUSTMENT ASSISTANCE.- The Deputy Administrator of BDSA 

is responsible for the administration of the program of trade adjustment assistance for firms authorized under title 

III of the Trade Expansion Act of 

1962. 

Office of Business Economics 

(1832 M Street NW., Washington, D.C., 20230)  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter VIII] The Office of Business Economics provides basic economic measures of the national economy, current analysis of the economic situation and business outlook, the United States balance of international payments, measurement and analysis of the factors affecting regional economic development in the United States, and general economic research on the functioning of the economy. For its analyses the Office develops economic and statistical indicators, and its national income and product work provides a basis for policy formulation by the Department, other executive agencies, and the Con- Co La Ce

gress, with respect to Government operations insofar as they affect economic movements. Its services to business are long established and well known through the official monthly journal 

Survey of Current Business. The Office of Business Economics organi zation includes six major operating units: National Income Division, Regional Economics Division, National Economics Division, Current Business Analysis Division, Business Structure Division, and the Balance of Payments Division. 

Bureau of the Census (Suitland, Md., 20233. Phone, 735-2000)  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter I] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

Constitution provides that an enumeration of the people shall be taken every 10 years in the manner in which the Congress shall direct. The act of 

March 6, 1902 (32 Stat. 51), established the Census Office as a permanent bureau. The act of February 14, 1903, transferred the Census Office to the Department of Commerce and La bor. Laws pertaining to the Bureau of the Census were codified as title 13, United States Code. 

PURPOSE.-Census taking was es tablished for the primary purpose of apportioning Representatives and direct taxes among the States on the basis of population. A population census has been taken decennially since 

1790. Other subjects have regularly been included as needs arose and statistical projects were assigned to the Bureau.

ORGANIZATION.-In addition to the headquarters at Suitland, Md., the

Bureau maintains a Census Opera tions Office at Jeffersonville, Ind., a

Personal Census Service Branch at 

Pittsburg, Kans., and 12 field organization offices.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-The 

Bureau is responsible for conducting periodic censuses, sample surveys, and other current data collections, and furnishing statistical services to other 

Government agencies.

MAJOR CENSUSES.-The schedule of major censuses regularly taken is: population and housing, once every 10 743-116°-65-20 years for years ending in 0; agriculture, once every 5 years for years ending in 

4 and 9, with drainage and irrigation for years ending in 9; governments, once every 5 years for years ending in 

2 and 7; and manufactures, mineral industries, business, and transportation, generally once every 5 years (dates have varied), scheduled in future for years ending in 2 and 7.

CURRENT PROGRAMS.-Data col lected at monthly, quarterly, or annual intervals provide up-to-date information on many subjects covered in the major censuses, on construction, and on U.S. foreign trade.

POPULATION.—The number, loca tion, and personal and family characteristics of the population, such as age, sex, race, marital status, place of birth, mother tongue of the foreign born, work status, occupation, education, mobility, and income, are included in the decennial census. 

The sample survey of the population provides current estimates of personal and family characteristics, population mobility, school enrollment, educational attainment, number and characteristics of households, income, and consumer buying indicators. 

Monthly estimates of the total population and annual estimates by age, color, and sex are made; annual estimates for States are prepared; periodically, estimates of the population of standard metropolitan statistical areas are prepared; and projections of the population are furnished periodically.

Special censuses in local areas are taken at the request and expense of the local governments.

HOUSING.-Statistics on the number and characteristics of housing units, such as number of rooms, persons per room, year built, tenure, value or rent, vacancy status, water supply, facilities, and equipment are provided by the decennial census of housing. 

Current housing statistics include data on rates, condition, and characteristics of housing vacancies, by geographic region.

AGRICULTURE. The agriculture cen sus provides data on the production and sale of farm products; farm and operator characteristics; farm labor, equipment, and facilities; cost of major farm inputs; use of agricultural chemicals; and farm values. The censuses of drainage and irrigation provide information on the number, characteristics, and extent of irrigation and drainage enterprises.

Statistics on cotton ginnings by State and county are published periodically during each season; detailed statistics on cotton production and distribution are published annually.

INDUSTRY.-The census of manufac tures provides data on employment, payrolls, materials consumption, shipments, value added by manufacture, inventories, capital expenditures, and gross book value of fixed assets and rent payments.

The Bureau conducts an annual survey of manufactures for intercensal years and a comprehensive monthly survey of manufacturers' shipments, inventories, and orders. It also issues about 100 series of monthly, quarterly, and annual reports on the current output, shipments, and stocks of the more important manufactured products.

The census of mineral industries provides measures of activity in the mining of coal, iron, and other metals and minerals, and the extraction of oil and gas including employment, payrolls, and value added in mining.

As a part of the 1963 economic census program, a census of commercial fisheries was taken to provide measures of employment, payrolls, vessels, gear, and value of catch.

BUSINESS. The census of business, covering retail and wholesale trade and selected services, provides data on number of establishments, sales, employment, and payroll, by kind of business; and on subjects such as employment size, sales or receipts size, and legal form of organization. It also provides data on retail trade in the central business districts of the important standard metropolitan statistical areas. 

Weekly and monthly estimates of retail sales, monthly estimates of retail accounts receivable and merchant wholesaler sales and inventories, and yearend inventories held by retailers are parts of the current statistics program.

TRANSPORTATION.-The first census of transportation was taken to provide 1963 data on major aspects of transportation including information about out-of-town trips by all modes of travel, manufacturers' shipments by all modes of transportation, truck inventory and use, and financial and operating data on for-hire bus and truck carriers not federally regulated. federally_regulated.

FOREIGN TRADE.-Reports on U.S. 

foreign trade include information on imports and exports in commodity and country detail; trade in gold and silver, trade with Puerto Rico and with

U.S. possessions, and trade by customs districts; shipments by vessel and by air; and vessel shipments by port of lading and unlading and flag of vessel. 

GOVERNMENTS.-The census of gov ernments makes available data on numbers and characteristics of governmental units, public employment and payrolls, tax valuations, and governmental finances by type of government. 

The program of current statistics on State and local governments provides annual data on finances and employment and on the financial operations of ter

employee-retirement systems administered by State and local governments, and quarterly data on State-local tax revenue. 

CONSTRUCTION.-Data are compiled monthly on housing starts, value of new construction put in place, new dwelling units authorized by local building permits, national and other aggregates of new residential construction authorized in permit-issuing places, and sales and unsold inventory of new houses.

Statistics are also provided on expenditures for residential additions, alterations, and repairs.

GENERAL COMPILATIONS.-With the Social Security Administration's assist ance, the Bureau issues periodically (annually beginning with 1964)

County Business Patterns. For addi tional publications, see Appendix B.

INTERNATIONAL STATISTICS.-The 

Bureau provides statistical consultation to foreign governments, arranges orientation programs for foreign visitors, and trains foreign technicians who are studying census and other statistical methods. Special studies are made in the field of foreign population and manpower and international statistical problems and methods. data for major censuses and periodic surveys, the field organization conducts special surveys at the request of Federal agencies and State and local governments.

DATA PROCESSING.-The Bureau has a large data-processing facility for handling statistics from its own censuses and surveys and for assisting other Government agencies with such services at cost. These services include providing computer tapes and punchcards containing machine-readable data, making special tabulations, and assisting in design and alteration of tabulating equipment. Machine-readable data and special tabulations are also made available to the public at cost, under appropriate circumstances.

STATISTICAL STAFF.-The Bureau has a staff qualified in the fields of sample survey design and methodology and procedural and program planning. 

This staff performs its functions in Bureau censuses and surveys and acts in an advisory capacity to other Government agencies.

ICE.-Searches are made of the decennial census records of population and certificates furnished to individuals for use as evidence of age and place of FIELD. In addition to collecting birth. 

Coast and Geodetic Survey  Reg ulations, Title 33, Chapter III] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

Coast and Geodetic Survey was established as the Coast Survey by the act of 

February 10, 1807 (2 Stat. 413), and was redesignated as the Coast and 

Geodetic Survey by the act of June 20, 1878 (20 Stat. 206, 215). The act of 

August 6, 1947 (61 Stat. 788, as amended, 74 Stat. 16; 33 U.S.C. 883a- 

883i), consolidates most of the previous authorizing legislation and sets forth the duties and functions of the 

Coast and Geodetic Survey.

PURPOSE. The bureau's mission is to provide charts and related information for the safe navigation of marine and air commerce, and to provide basic geodetic, geophysical, and oceanographic data for engineering and scientific purposes and for commercial, industrial, and defense needs.

ORGANIZATION.-The Coast and 

Geodetic Survey headquarters organization consists of the Office of the Di rector and the following: Office of 

Oceanography, consisting of the Op erations Division, Facilities Division,

and Marine Data Division; Office of 

Physical Sciences, consisting of the 

Geodesy Division, Photogrammetry Division, Electronic Computing Division, Geomagnetism Division, and Seis mology Division;

Office of Research and Development; Office of Cartog raphy, consisting of the Nautical Chart 

Division, Aeronautical Chart Division, Reproduction Division, and Distribution Division; and Office of Administration, consisting of the Budget and 

Finance Division, Administrative and Technical Services Division, Personnel Division, Management and Organiza tion Division, and Engineering Division.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-The 

Coast and Geodetic Survey performs the following activities or functions, including the analysis and processing of the collected data and publication of the results thereof: (1) hydrographic, photogrammetric, and oceanographic surveys, including tide and current observations; (2) geodetic control surveys and the establishment of the basic network of horizontal and vertical control for the United States; (3) other field surveys for nautical and aeronautical charting purposes; (4) geomagnetic, seismological, gravity, and astronomic observations; (5) operation of a seismic sea wave warning system serving all Pacific areas; (6) basic research to increase knowledge in the earth sciences and of related space phenomena; and (7) applied research and development in cartography, instrumentation, survey methods, and processing and analytical techniques, to improve operating efficiency.

The survey functions enumerated above are accomplished through the operation of survey vessels, mobile field parties, aircraft, observatories and laboratories, and tide gage stations.

In addition, a system of field offices and two ship bases comprise the bureau's field organization. The bureau's headquarters organization directs and coordinates all field functions and in addition performs the final analysis and processing of the collected data. 

The end function performed by the bureau is the reproduction and distribution of the survey results and other collected or discovered knowledge.

Principal end products include: nautical and aeronautical charts, tide prediction tables, other navigation publications, and geodetic control data in printed form. Besides these, other publications, copies of original records, and special compilations embodying results of regular program work and research in the fields of geodesy, oceanography, cartography, geomagnetism, and seismology are made available.

CREATION AND Community Relations Service AUTHORITY.-The Community Relations Service was es tablished July 2, 1964, in and as a part of the Department of Commerce by title X of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 

(78 Stat. 241; 42 U.S.C. 2000a note).

PURPOSE.—The Service provides as sistance to communities and persons in I resolving disputes, disagreements, or I difficulties relating to discriminatory practices based on race, color, or national origin which impair the rights of persons in such communities under the 

1 Constitution or laws of the United =States or which affect or may affect interstate commerce. The Service may offer its services whenever peaceful relations among the citizens of the community involved are threatened either upon the request of officials or other interested persons, or upon its own motion. Further, the Service in performing its function is directed to seek and utilize the cooperation of appropriate State or local, public or private agencies.

ORGANIZATION.-The program of the Community Relations Service is con ducted by the following offices:

Con ciliation, Community Action, and Media Relations. 

ACTIVITIES. The principal function of the Service is to assist communities in conciliating disputes and disagreements and in developing programs to prevent racial crises. This includes undertaking post-conciliation efforts at the local level in those communities in which the Service has been involved in actively conciliating disputes. These preventive measures are carried out in cooperation with public and private organizations at the national, State, and local level. In all these activities the Service is assisted by the 450 members of the National Citizens Commit tee for Community Relations. 

The above functions are supported by a national program of public information administered in part in cooperation with relevant professional associations representing the media, aimed at achieving wider understanding and acceptance of both the provisions and principles of the 

Civil Rights Act of 1964.

Office of Foreign Commercial Services 

The Office of Foreign Commercial 

Services was established by the Secretary of Commerce on February 1, 1963, by Department Order 183.

It provides support for all the international programs of the Department of Commerce by carrying out the Department's responsibilities relating to foreign commercial services and commercial officer representation abroad.

Working closely with the State De partment to strengthen commercial services within the framework of a unified Foreign Service, the Office implements the provisions of the State- 

Commerce Agreement of November 

1961 on international commercial activities. 

The Office comprises five divisions: 

Overseas Personnel, Foreign Activities Management, Performance Evalua tion, Training Programs, and Foreign 

Communications. 

As the point of direction or coordination between organization units of the Department of Commerce and the 

Department of State and the U.S. 

Foreign Service, the Office performs the following functions: (1) recommends personnel assignments and participates in the selection and control of manpower in the Foreign Service with respect to commercial activities; (2) evaluates the effectiveness of commercial reporting and program operations, and of the performance of personnel assigned to carry out this work abroad; (3) coordinates or initiates and conducts improved programs for training commercial officers and Foreign Service local employees performing commercial work; (4) coordinates and maintains communications between the Department of Commerce and posts abroad; (5) plans, directs, and coordinates the budgeting, staffing, assignment, recruitment, and related activities of the commercial specialist program as stipulated in the State- Commerce Agreement; and (6) develops guidelines covering the functions and responsibilities of commercial officers abroad, and initiates or coordinates instructions to overseas posts.

Bureau of International Commerce 

 Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter III] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Bureau of International Commerce 

(BIC), center of the Department's international commercial activities, was established by the Secretary on February 1, 1963, by Department Order 

182, under authority provided by Re organization Plan 5 of 1950. 

BIC promotes the foreign trade of the United States and assists U.S. business in its operations abroad.

PURPOSE. The prime objective of the Bureau is to increase U.S. exports and thus reduce the deficit in the U.S. balance of international payments. It advances this objective by: (1) providing services and information which make it easier for American businessmen to trade abroad; (2) operating trade centers, organizing trade missions, running trade fair exhibits and other marketing devices to promote U.S. goods in markets abroad; (3) working with other Government agencies and international organizations to create a climate in which international trade and investment can flourish; (4) presenting the views of traders and investors in governmental councils; and (5) working out policies and procedures which make it simpler and more profitable to do business abroad.

The Bureau also administers the Export Control Act of 1949, as amended (50 U.S.C., App. 2021, 2024) to prevent the export of strategic U.S. materials, equipment, and technical data to Sino-Soviet bloc countries where their use could be detrimental to the 

United States. 

In addition, it administers the China 

Trade Act of 1922, as amended (15)

U.S.C. 141 et seq.) to promote U.S. 

exports to Hong Kong and Taiwan. 

ORGANIZATION.-BIC is headed by a Director who is responsible to the 

Assistant Secretary for Domestic and

International Business. 

The Office of the Director includes the Compliance Commissioner, the Executive Secretariat of the Advisory 

Committee on Export Policy, the Ex ecutive Secretariat of the Foreign- Trade Zones Board, and the Interna tional Organizations Staff. There are five other Offices in the Bureau: Com mercial and Financial Policy, International Regional Economics, International Trade Promotion, International Investment, and Export Control. 

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES COMPLIANCE COMMISSIONER.-The Compliance Commissioner conducts hearings and performs other duties with respect to administrative compliance proceedings involving export control violation cases.

ADVISORY COMMITTEE ON EXPORT POLICY (ACEP) EXECUTIVE SECRETAR- LAT. The Secretariat serves ACEP, the interdepartmental committee established under the Export Control Act to provide information and advice to the Secretary of Commerce on export licenses, policies, and programs. 

FOREIGN-TRADE ZONES BOARD EXECU- TIVE SECRETARIAT.-This unit conducts regulatory, administrative, and techni cal affairs of the Foreign-Trade Zones 

Board, as required by the Foreign- 

Trade Zones Act (19 U.S.C. 81a-81u) 

which provides for the establishment, operation, and maintenance of foreigntrade zones in or adjacent to ports of entry of the United States.

The zones are approved sites where foreign and domestic merchandise may be brought without being subject to U.S. customs laws governing entry or payment of duties. Facilities are available to foreign as well as American business firms. They afford advantages to firms engaged in manufacturing, export, re-export, import, and transshipment.

Six zones and two industrial subzones are operated currently in New 

York, Louisiana, California, Washington, Ohio, and Puerto Rico. A new general-purpose zone is now being established in Honolulu, Hawaii.

INTERNATIONAL 

ORGANIZATIONS 

STAFF. This is the liaison office for the Department of Commerce with the Department of State on international organizations. The staff participates in the nomination and selection of U.S. delegates to represent the Department at international conferences, preconference planning and preparation, coordination, and policy review of material for use by U.S. delegations.

OFFICE OF COMMERCIAL AND FINAN- CIAL POLICY (OCFP).-This office de velops and recommends the Department's international commercial and financial policies and programs. 

It contributes to preparations for and participation in international trade negotiations, advises the Presi dent's Special Representative for 

Trade Negotiations on the business interest in reduction in foreign tariff and other trade barriers, and participates in developing the U.S. business interest in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and the Or ganization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD); develops recommendations on foreign tariff concessions, customs valuation procedures, border taxes, and other concessions to be requested of foreign countries; presents the view of the Department and industry in interagency consultations and international negotiating conferences; develops recommendations and participates in international discussions pertaining to international commodity and material policies, marketing arrangements, and commodity study groups; proposes revisions of U.S. Government policies, regulations, and procedures to maintain the competitiveness of U.S. firms in international operations; recommends action to coun teract arbitrary and discriminatory treatment of American business; reconciles business needs with U.S. policy aims in the fields of restrictive business practices; presents the American business viewpoint in developing policies for loans and views on specific loans made by the Export-Import 

Bank, Agency for International Development, and international lending organizations; proposes and reviews policies promoting U.S. private investment in less developed countries; insures consideration of export expansion in the development of transportation policy by Government agencies; makes recommendations concerning discriminatory ocean freight rates and other transportation cost factors adversely affecting exports; provides staff sup port to the interagency National Facilitation Committee; and provides advice and assistance to U.S. business in the field of international insurance. 

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL REGIONAL ECONOMICS (OIRE).-This office pro vides businessmen with information on marketing, investment, and economic conditions in more than a hundred countries and regions; helps established exporters find new business abroad and introduces new or potential exporters to world markets; helps businessmen determine their export potentials by supplying them with data on conditions or policies affecting their ability to compete in particular markets; prepares statistical analyses on trade between the United States and other countries as well as among foreign countries and is the primary source for analyses of trade statistics of foreign countries; and works with the U.S. 

Foreign Service to remove foreign governments' tariff and nontariff restrictions which make it difficult for U.S. exporters to compete in Overseas markets. 

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL TRADE PROMOTION (OITP).-This office es tablishes trade centers and presents export promotion exhibitions at such cen- S. ركة 5 Co

ters, presents exhibitions at international trade fairs, operates the trade mission programs, and provides basic commercial information to facilitate international trade.

U.S. trade centers located in London, Frankfurt, Bangkok, Tokyo, Milan, and Stockholm are permanent show-and-sell facilities in overseas marketing areas where interest in buying U.S. made goods is combined with purchasing power.

U.S. commercial exhibitions are staged at international trade fairs abroad to open new markets for U.S. products and to secure overseas agencies for future business.

U.S. National Exhibitions are pre sented generally at international trade fairs in conjunction with the United States Information Agency and other 

U.S. Government agencies to demon strate U.S. social, cultural, and economic accomplishments.

U.S. trade missions are sent into promising world markets to develop sales and business opportunities for U.S. firms. Official trade missions, each composed of several businessmen and two Commerce Department officers, are organized annually.

Each mission carries hundreds of specific business proposals from American firms directly to businessmen abroad. Trade opportunities developed by the missions are open to all U.S. 

industry. Industry-operated, Govern ment-approved missions undertake similar trade promotion activities with specific regard to the immediate interests of the sponsoring group.

Mobile trade fairs developed by private interests to show and sell U.S. products abroad are aided financially and are provided some technical support.

Business information centers are maintained at certain international commercial fairs when a larger participation is not feasible. Booths are established with the cooperation of commercial officers in the U.S. Foreign

Service. 

Sample product displays, a device to facilitate the selection of distribution agents, are maintained under the supervision of the commercial attaché at some Foreign Service posts.

Specific business services provided by OITP include: commercial intelligence to help U.S. firms locate potential customers or representatives overseas; information on foreign distributors, importers, and agents; assistance, with the cooperation of the Foreign Service, in settling trade disputes between U.S. and foreign firms; and the maintenance of an Agency Index to identify suppliers of U.S. merchandise in foreign markets.

OFFICE OF INTERNATIONAL INVEST- 

MENT (OII).-This office identifies investment opportunities in the developing countries and brings them to the attention of U.S. business; encourages firms abroad to make investments in the United States, especially in areas of heavy unemployment; promotes the licensing of foreign technology to American firms; and publishes for the benefit of American industry opportunities for investment and licensing ventures in the industrialized countries of the free world.

OFFICE OF EXPORT CONTROL (OEC).- 

This office administers the export control program to keep unfriendly nations from obtaining U.S. commodities. or technical data that would contribute significantly to their military or economic potential to the detriment of U.S. security or welfare; uses export controls to protect the domestic economy against excessive drain of scarce materials and to further the foreign policy of the U.S.; conducts educational programs to enlist support of the U.S. business community for effective export control; and investigates suspected violations of export regulations and develops evidence.

Maritime Administration (General Accounting Office Building, 441 G Street NW., Washington, D.C., 20235. 

Phone, STerling 3-5200)  Reg ulations, Title 32A, Chapter XVIII (National Shipping Authority) and XIX (Office of the Maritime Administrator); Title 46, Chapter II (Maritime Administration and Maritime Subsidy Board)] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

Maritime Administration was estab lished by Reorganization Plan 21 of 

1950, effective May 24, 1950, as one of the successor agencies to the former 

United States Maritime Commission. 

PURPOSE.- -The Maritime Adminis tration administers programs authorized by the Merchant Marine Act, 1936, as amended, and related shipping statutes to aid in the development, promotion, and operation of an American merchant marine, so that it will be (a) adequate to carry the Nation's domestic waterborne commerce and a substantial portion of its foreign commerce during peacetime; (b) capable of serving as a naval and military auxiliary in time of war or national emergency; (c) owned and operated under U.S. flag by citizens of the United States, so far as may be practicable; and (d) composed of the best equipped, safest, and most suitable types of ships manned by a trained and efficient citizen personnel.

ORGANIZATION.-The Maritime Ad ministration is headed by a Maritime

Administrator, who is appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate. Its headquarters organization in Washington,

D.C., is composed of an Office of Program Planning, Office of Budget and 

Management, Office of Public Information, Office of Statistics, Office of Personnel Management, Office of the General Counsel, Office of the Comptroller, Office of Property and Supply, Office of Ship Construction, Office of Research and Development, Office of Ship Operations, and Office of Government Aid. 

There is established within the 

Maritime Administration a Maritime Subsidy Board, composed of the Mari time Administrator, who serves as 

Chairman, the Deputy Maritime Administrator, and the General Counsel, each of whom acts pursuant to direct authority from the Secretary of Commerce. The Board makes, amends, and terminates contracts for operating-differential and construction-differential subsidies. It conducts hearings and makes determinations antecedent to these actions; and it investigates and determines the relative costs of constructing ships in the United States and in foreign countries and of oper ating ships under United States and competitive foreign flags. 

The Maritime Administrator is also vested with the residual powers and authorities of the Director, National 

Shipping Authority, which was established by the Secretary of Commerce on March 13, 1951, for the purpose of organizing and directing emergency merchant ship operations in the national interest.

In the districts, the Offices of the 

Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific Coast Directors located at New York, N.Y., New Orleans, La., and San Francisco,

Calif., are responsible for all field offices and programs of the Maritime Administration within their respective coast areas, except ship construction and maritime training. 

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO SHIP- PING. The Maritime Administration administers the operating-differential 31 32

and construction-differential subsidy programs and other Government aids to merchant shipping, authorized by law. Under these programs, the Government pays the difference between certain costs of operating ships under U.S.-flag and foreign competitive flags, on essential foreign trade routes; and the difference (not to exceed a certain percent of the total cost) between the costs of constructing ships in the United States and in foreign shipbuilding centers. The Government also pays the cost of national defense features incorporated in the ships that are certified by the Department of the Navy as necessary for national defense. 

In addition, the Administration insures mortgages and/or loans made by private lending institutions to finance the construction, reconstruction, and reconditioning of ships; and it acquires old ships in exchange for more modern and efficient ships or for allowances of credit on the construction of new ships.

The Administration also investigates and determines ocean services, routes, and lines essential for the development and maintenance of the foreign commerce of the United 

States; and the type, size, speed, and other requirements of ships to provide adequate service on such routes. The operators who are awarded operatingdifferential subsidy contracts are required to maintain regular services on these routes.

The Administration assists the shipping industry to generate increased trade and cargo shipments for U.S.-flag ships. Shippers, freight forwarders, and manufacturers are encouraged to use U.S.-flag shipping in conformance with sections 101 and 212(d) of the act of 1936, as an aid to the American fleet, and to assist in developing a credit position in balance of payments. 

RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT. - The Maritime Administration con ducts research and development activities in the maritime field, including cargo handling, development and utilization of new ship designs, marine transportation systems, advanced propulsion concepts, and ship management techniques. The objectives of this program are to improve the efficiency and economy of operations of the American merchant marine and to promote more rapid technical advancement of it. 

SHIPBUILDING AND DESIGN.-The Maritime Administration develops plans and specifications for prototype ships. It encourages and participates in the development of plans and designs by subsidized operators under their ship replacement programs, and by applicants for Government aid covering ships proposed to be constructed or converted. It inspects ships during the course of work to assure conformance with approved plans and specifications. 

To carry out the national maritime policy, the Maritime Administration, with the approval of the President, constructs, reconstructs, and reconditions ships for Government account. 

The Administration is authorized to sell these ships, charter them to private operators, or utilize them for Government operation.

SHIP OPERATIONS AND REPAIR. 

The Maritime Administration charters 

Government-owned ships to United States operators when it is determined that such charters will promote the national maritime policy. During national emergencies it requisitions or procures for operation or for charter ships owned by citizens of the United States or under construction, and it determines requirements for and allocates ships to meet the needs of national defense programs. In connection with the foregoing the Maritime Administration prescribes ship operations and ship repair standards and administers such standards under the provisions of charter and general agency agreements and operatingdifferential subsidy contracts. 

NATIONAL DEFENSE RESERVE FLEET.-The Maritime Administra-

tion maintains national defense reserve fleets of Government-owned ships determined by the Maritime Administration and the Department of Defense to be essential for national defense. It sells or otherwise disposes of ships determined to be nonessential for national defense purposes.

OPERATION OF WAREHOUSES.-The Maritime Administration maintains and operates four warehouses for the storage of marine equipment required for the reactivation, repair, and operation of ships.

RESERVE SHIPYARD.-The Maritime 

Administration maintains a shipyard in an inactive condition to be used for ship construction and repair in national emergencies.

MARITIME TRAINING.-The Maritime Administration operates the U. S. 

Merchant Marine Academy, Kings 

Point, N. Y. Academy graduates are licensed as merchant marine officers and qualified for commissions as en signs in the U. S. Naval Reserve. The 

Administration also administers grant-in-aid program for the five maritime academies operated by five 

States: California, Maine, Massachusetts, New York, and Texas.

CONSTRUCTION RESERVE FUNDS. 

Under regulations jointly issued by the 

Secretary of Commerce and the Secre tary of the Treasury, American shipowners may deposit proceeds from the sale or loss of ships and earnings from operation of ships in tax-deferred funds, for use in the construction or acquisition of new ships. 

TRANSFER OF SHIPS TO ALIENS.- The Maritime Administration regu lates the sales to aliens, and transfers to foreign registry, of ships owned in whole or in part by citizens of the United States and documented under the laws of the United States, and, in time of war or national emergency, of ships so owned without regard to documentation. 

WAR RISK INSURANCE.-The Mari time Administration is authorized to provide Government war risk insur ance of merchant ships when adequate insurance cannot be obtained on reasonable terms and conditions from private insurance companies of the 

United States.

Kings Point, N. Y.  Reg ulations, Title 37, Chapters I, III] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.- -The 

Patent Office was established to administer the patent laws enacted by Congress in accordance with Article I, section 8, of the Constitution. The first of these laws was enacted April 10, 1790 (1 Stat. 109). General revisions of the patent laws were made on 

July 4, 1836 (5 Stat. 117), and on 

July 8, 1870 (16 Stat. 198). These and

other acts of Congress relating to patents were revised and codified, effective January 1, 1953, by the act of 

July 19, 1952 (66 Stat. 792; 35 U.S.C. 

1-293). In addition to the patent laws, the Patent Office administers the Federal trademark laws, the present Estatute being the act approved July 5, 1946 (60 Stat. 427; 15 U.S.C. 1051, as amended).

PURPOSE. To administer the patent laws as they relate to the granting of letters patent for inventions, and the trademark laws as they relate to the registration of trademarks.

ORGANIZATION.-The major organi zational units of the Patent Office consist of the Office of the Commissioner of Patents, the Board of Appeals, the Board of Patent Interferences, the Patent Examing Corps, the Office of Administration, the Office of Information Services, the Office of International 

Patent and Trademark Affairs, the Office of Research and Development, the Office of Patent Classification, the Scientific Library; with respect to trademarks there is the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board, and the 

Trademark Examining Operation. 

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-The 

Patent Office examines applications for patents to ascertain if the applicants are entitled to patents under the law, and grants the patents when they are so entitled; it publishes and disseminates patented matter, records the assignment of patents, maintains a Scientific Library and a search file of U.S. and foreign patents for public use, and supplies copies of patents and official records of the Patent Office. Similar functions are performed in carrying out the statutory provisions for the registration of trademarks.

National Bureau of Standards 

(Connecticut Avenue at Van Ness Street NW., Washington, D.C., 20234.

Phone, Emerson 2-4040)  Reg ulations, Title 15, Chapter II] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

National Bureau of Standards was established by act of Congress of March 3, 1901 (31 Stat. 1449, as amended; 15 

U.S.C. 271-286). The Bureau was initially part of the Treasury Department and was transferred to the Department of Commerce and Labor on its creation in 1903. 

PURPOSE. The National Bureau of 

Standards is a principal focal point in the Federal Government for assuring maximum application of the physical and engineering sciences to the advancement of technology in industry and commerce. To this end the Bureau conducts research and provides central national services in four broad pro- -gram areas: (1) basic measurement standards, (2) materials research, (3) engineering standards and applied technology, and (4) radio propagation.

ORGANIZATION.-The Bureau is com posed of four major organization units, each of which is concerned with one of the aforementioned program areas. 

These units are: 

(1) The Institute for Basic Stand ards which includes a series of twelve divisions, each serving a classical subject matter area of science and engineering; 

(2) The Institute for Materials Re search which consists of six divisions organized primarily by technical field, the Office of Standard Reference Materials and a Materials Evaluation 

Laboratory; 

(3) The Institute for Applied Tech nology which includes a technology center, eight technical divisions, and a clearinghouse for scientific and technical information; and 

(4) The Central Radio Propaga tion Laboratory which comprises a series of four divisions located at Boulder, Colo.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES INSTITUTE FOR BASIC STANDARDS.- 

This institute provides the central basis within the United States of a complete and consistent system of coordinates physical measurement, that system with the measurement systems of other nations, and furnishes essential services leading to accurate and uniform physical measurements throughout the Nation's scientific community, industry, and commerce. 

Its principal activities include the development and maintenance of the national standards for physical measurement; determination of fundamental physical constants; research on fundamental physical phenomena; research and development on measurement techniques and instrumentation; and the calibration of instruments in terms of the national standards. It also administers, through the Office of Standard Reference Data, the National 

Standard Reference Data System which provides critically evaluated data in the physical sciences on a national basis. 

INSTITUTE FOR MATERIALS RE- 

SEARCH.-This institute assists and stimulates industry in the development of new and improved products by supplying increased understanding of the basic properties and behavior of materials and making available reliable quantitative information on the performance of materials. These functions are accomplished through research on the properties of matter and materials; the development of techniques for the

preparation of experimental materials and for the measurement of their properties; the development of criteria to evaluate the performance characteristics of materials; and the development, production, and distribution of standard reference materials. 

INSTITUTE FOR APPLIED TECHNOL- 

OGY. This institute provides for the creation of appropriate opportunities for the use and application of technology within the Federal Government and within the civilian sector of American industry. The primary functions of the Institute may be broadly classified as programs relating to technical information and measurement programs related to the use of technology.

The Institute provides a central clearinghouse for the collection and dissemination of scientific and technical information generated by Government research. Its technical divisions provide a basis for cooperation between public and private organizations leading to the development of performance criteria and test methods for evaluating such criteria.

CENTRAL RADIO PROPAGATION LABO- RATORY.-The Laboratory is the cen tral agency of the Federal Government for the collection, analysis, and dissemination of information on the propagation of electromagnetic waves along the surface of the earth, in the atmosphere, and in space, and performs studies looking toward new techniques for the efficient use and conservation of the electromagnetic spectrum. The Laboratory conducts basic research on the nature of electromagnetic waves and the media through which they are transmitted; studies electromagnetic propagation mechanisms; provides advisory services on frequency utilization and telecommunications systems; and issues predictions of ionospheric radio propagation conditions.

United States Travel Service 

(1666 Connecticut Avenue NW., Washington, D.C., 20230)

CREATION.-The United States Travel Service was established June 

29, 1961, pursuant to the International

Travel Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 129; 22 

U.S.C. 2121 note) as a primary organization unit in the Department of Commerce.

PURPOSE. The purposes of the 

Travel Service are to develop, plan, and carry out a comprehensive program designed to stimulate and encourage travel to the United States by residents of foreign countries for the purpose of study, culture, recreation, business, and other activities as a means of promoting friendly understanding and good will among peoples of foreign countries and of the United States; encourage the development of tourist facilities, low-cost unit tours, and other arrangements within the United States for meeting the requirements of foreign visitors; foster and encourage the widest possible distribution of the benefits of travel at the cheapest rates between foreign countries and the United States consistent with sound economic principles; encourage the simplification, reduction, or elimination of barriers to travel, and the facilitation of international travel generally; collect, publish, and provide for the exchange of statistics and technical information, including schedules of meetings, fairs, and other attractions, relating to international travel and tourism.

ORGANIZATION. The program of the Travel Service is conducted by the following divisions: Travel Promotion, Facilitation and Planning, and Visitor 

Services.

In addition to these divisions, St

RE

nine overseas offices have been established to stimulate tourist travel. These offices are located in London, England; 

Paris, France; Frankfurt, Germany; 

Rome, Italy; Tokyo, Japan; Sydney, Australia; São Paulo, Brazil; Bogotá, Colombia; and Mexico City, Mexico.

ACTIVITIES.-The major share of ap propriated funds are used to provide tools and materials for distribution by the overseas offices, such as advertisements, pamphlets, brochures, posters, slides, and films, in order to help the prospective traveler study and measure the United States against other competitive destinations. 

In addition, the following activities are being carried out: editorial support of the program through domestic and foreign media endorsing the 

United States as a tourist destination; encouragement to State and local community groups for the establishment of "host" services throughout the country; development of ways and means of overcoming barriers to travel; and a study of the economic aspects of tourism and patterns of international travel. 

Weather Bureau (M Street bet. Twenty-fourth and Twenty-fifth Streets NW., Washington D.C., 20235. 

Phone, 965-2400)  

Regulations, Title 15, Chapter V] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-An act of October 1, 1890 (26 Stat. 653; 15 

U.S.C. 311), established the United 

States Weather Bureau in the Depart ment of Agriculture. The President's Reorganization Plan IV of 1940 trans ferred the Bureau and its functions to the Department of Commerce. Addi tional legislation and executive decisions have broadened the Bureau's activities, emphasized its responsibility for providing basic weather services to support all Federal agencies and user interests (particularly civil aviation), and authorized the use of space satellites for meteorological purposes.

PURPOSE.-The Weather Bureau is responsible for the national meteoro- 

Elogical service. This service includes reporting the weather and climate of the United States and its possessions, and issuing forecasts and warnings of weather and flood conditions that affect the Nation's safety, welfare, and economy.

ORGANIZATION.-Approximately 325 

field offices are operated by the 

Weather Bureau at cities and airports 743-116-65-21 throughout the United States, in

Puerto Rico, and on some of the islands of the Pacific Ocean. In addition, more than 12,000 substations, most of them staffed by volunteers observers, provide less complex reports and observations to supplement those taken by the principal principal Weather Bureau offices.

Ocean weather stations are maintained by the Bureau in both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans and in the Gulf of Mexico.

Supervision of field stations in the United States is exercised through regional offices located at New York, N.Y.; Fort Worth, Tex.; Kansas City, Mo.; Salt Lake City, Utah; Anchorage, Alaska; and Honolulu, Hawaii. 

Headquarters functions located in the Washington, D.C., area consist of technical program divisions, a research and development organization, administrative and housekeeping activities, and the National Weather 

Satellite Center. 

A National Meteorological Center, which analyzes weather conditions. over the Northern Hemisphere and

prepares guidance material for both civil and military forecast offices, is operated by the Bureau near Washington, D.C. 

Processing and archiving of meteorological reports for climatological purposes is performed at the Bureau's 

National Weather Records Center, 

Asheville, N.C.

FUNCTIONS AND ACTIVITIES.-To carry out its statutory responsibilities, the Weather Bureau: 

Maintains basic networks of weather-measuring stations, makes weather analyses and forecasts, and conducts climatic studies and archiving work. 

Provides public warnings, forecasts, and related information concerning the weather of the United States and adjacent waters. In the interest of safety and economy, the Weather Bureau also provides forecasts and warnings for aviation, agricultural, and forest-protection interests. 

Issues flood warnings, river stage forecasts, and water supply forecasts covering most of the principal rivers and tributaries of the United States. 

Collects, analyzes, and publishes information concerning the climate of the United States, the oceans, and certain foreign areas. 

Conducts basic and applied meteorological research to improve weather warnings and forecasts. This includes studies of worldwide wind circulation, cloud physics, atmospheric processes, and other meteorological phenomena, as well as research aimed at improving meteorological instruments and weather communications systems. 

Has the responsibility of establishing and operating a satellite system for the continuous observation of worldwide weather systems. Information received from weather satellites is processed and disseminated to users in the United States and the international community.

[For regulations codified under Department of Labor, see Code of 

Federal Regulations, Title 48, Chapter IV] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Department of Labor, ninth executive department, was created by act ap proved March 4, 1913 (37 Stat. 

736; 5 U.S.C. 611). A Bureau of

Labor was first created by Congress in 1884 under the Interior Department. The Bureau of Labor later became independent as a Department of Labor without executive rank. It again returned to bureau status in the De partment of Commerce and Labor which was created by act of February 

14, 1903 (32 Stat. 827; 5 U. S. C. 591).

Additional duties related to the statutory functions of the Department of Labor subsequently have been assigned to the Department by new legislation and by Executive order.

PURPOSE.-The Department of La bor is charged, among other things, with administering and enforcing statutes designed to advance the public interest by promoting the welfare of the wage earners of the United States, improving their working conditions, and advancing their opportunities for profitable employment.

ORGANIZATION.-All functions of the 

Department are vested in the Secre tary of Labor. The structure of the 

Department is shown in the organization chart which appears on page 609. 

Secretary of Labor 

 Reg ulations, Title 29, Subtitle A] The Secretary is the head of the De partment of Labor and the principal adviser to the President on the development and execution of policies and the administration and enforcement of laws relating to wage earners, their working conditions, and their employment opportunities. He is responsible for all activities of the Department of 

Labor. 

OFFICE OF LEGISLATIVE LIAISON.- The Special  for Legislative Affairs coordinates, su pervises, and directs all legislative activities of the Department including contacts with the Congress and pres-

entation of legislative programs and views to the Congress. 

OFFICE OF INFORMATION, PUBLICA- TIONS, AND REPORTS.-The Director of Information, Publications, and Reports plans and directs all informational activities of the Department, advises the Secretary on the public information aspect of the Department's programs, and develops and maintains appropriate liaison with other agencies and organizations and with foreign countries in connection with the work of the Department. He supervises departmental relations with press, radio, television, and other public information media, and is clearance officer for all Labor Department releases. 

WAGE APPEALS BOARD.-The Wage Appeals Board acts on behalf of the Secretary of Labor in deciding appeals on questions of law and fact, taken in the discretion of the Board (1) from wage determinations issued by the Solicitor under the Davis-Bacon Act and its related prevailing wage statutes; (2) debarments under the Depart ment's regulations Part 5 (29 CFR 

Part 5), which implement Reorganization Plan 14 of 1950; (3) under the

Department's regulations, Part 5, disputes concerning the payment of prevailing wage rates or proper classifications which involve significant sums of money, large groups of employees, or novel or unusual situations; and (4) recommendations by Federal agencies for appropriate adjustments of liquidated damages which are assessed under the Contract Work Hours Standards Act. 

Under Secretary of Labor The Under Secretary of Labor is the alternate of the Secretary in the discharge of all the Secretary's_responsibilities. He serves as Acting Secretary in the Secretary's absence. 

DEPUTY UNDER SECRETARY OF LA- BOR.-The Deputy Under Secretary assists the Secretary and the Under 

Secretary by reviewing and appraising program operations of the Department, seeing that policies are properly reflected in programs, and that policy objectives are achieved. He has responsibility for policy direction, planning, and supervision of all departmental programs and bureau activities in the areas of domestic, foreign, and migratory farm labor. The Manpower

The Manpower Administration is composed of the office and bureaus described in the following paragraphs. 

Office of Manpower, Automation, and Training 

This office performs planning, research, and evaluation functions. It develops and recommends plans for a comprehensive national manpower program that will guide and make possible the coordination of decisions and activities of the Department of Labor, and in addition provide guidelines for other Federal agencies, employers, labor unions, professional organizations, State and local governments (including those engaged in educational activity), private educational institutions, and others in making and executing manpower decisions. This includes the development of policies and standards for implementing such manpower development and utilization programs as enumerated above. other bureaus of the Department or other Government or private agencies to conduct high-priority, pathfinding research to augment existing research in the manpower area. The objective is to identify the many ramifications and the dimensions of the manpower problems of the Nation and to seek through research, adequate solutions to these problems. It plans and directs developmental and experimental studies in all areas of manpower and automation to find solutions to problems which significantly affect the Nation's ability to eliminate persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment and to evaluate the impact of and benefits and problems created by automation and other forms of technological progress. It plans and develops a program to increase and expand knowledge of how occupational competence that will aid in eliminating unemployment and underemployment is achieved.

The Office appraises the manpower requirements and resources of the Nation and develops policies, objectives, and standards to deal with the problems of persistent and other types of unemployment and underemployment, while considering such factors as current and prospective manpower shortages, dislocations in the economy arising from automation or other technological developments, foreign competition, relocation of industry, shifts in market demands, and other changes in the structure of the economy. 

The Office provides leadership in planning, evaluating, and coordinating the manpower and automation research and related statistic programs in the Department and identifies the need for and plans, conducts, or arranges for The Office prepares materials for the President's and the Secretary of Labor's Annual Manpower Reports together with recommendations for action. It prepares the Secretary of

Labor's annual report to the Congress on training and research activities conducted pursuant to the Manpower Development and Training Act of 1962, as amended, including an evaluation of the effectiveness of such activities. It provides technical manpower information to the public, professional groups, unions, employers, and Government agencies on the nature of manpower problems and programs. It maintains a clearinghouse of technical and research information on manpower, automation, and training. 

The Office coordinates the program planning and development activities of the Department of Labor bureaus. 

providing manpower programs for the aging, minority groups, the handicapped and youth, and insures that the bureaus and offices providing manpower programs take into account the da dard ne re pera DOW

The Office promotes and develops experimental and demonstration manpower projects through contracts with public and private organizations for special worker groups with emphasis on disadvantaged persons, unique or emerging occupations and programs which are national or regional in character; develops objectives, policies, and standards governing such projects; and contracts with colleges and universities to conduct followup studies to determine whether the programs are meeting the occupational training needs of those they serve. It has the prime responsibility for converting experimental and demonstration results. to operational policies and procedures for use by governmental agencies with manpower responsibilities. 

The Office is responsible for evalu ating plans, programs, progress, and results of the elements of the comprehensive manpower program; examining and reporting on special difficulties which interfere with achievement of general objectives; and providing appraisals of the adequacy of programs to meet foreseeable manpower needs. 

Bureau of Apprenticeship and

Training 

The National Apprenticeship Act was passed in 1937 to bring together employers and labor for the formulation of programs of apprenticeship. 

The Bureau of Apprenticeship and 

Training carries out the objectives of the act in conformance with policies determined by the Federal Committee on Apprenticeship, an 11-member committee appointed by the Secretary of Labor and composed of 5 representatives each from management and labor and 1 from the U.S. Office of Education. 

The Bureau promotes the establishment and improvement of apprenticeship and other on-the-job training programs and provides technical assistance and training aids where necessary. Its functions are to aid management and labor in recognizing the need for apprenticeship. Through field representatives in each State the Bureau works closely with employers, labor, vocational schools, and others concerned with apprenticeship programs throughout industry.
