Bureau of Employment Security 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 20, Chapter V] 

The Bureau's responsibilities are related to the administration of a nationwide system of public employment services, State unemployment insurance programs, Federal unemployment compensation programs, and special manpower programs designed to relieve the effects of unemployment and to promote maximum utilization of the Nation's manpower. The legislative bases for the Bureau's operations include the Wagner-Peyser Act, the 

Federal Unemployment Tax Act, titles III, IX, XII, and XV of the Social Security Act, the Farm Labor Contrac tor Registration Act, various provisions in the Immigration and Nationality Act, the Area Redevelopment Act, the Manpower Development and Training Act, the Vocational Education Act of 1963, the Trade Expansion Act, the Economic Opportunity Act, and the Civil Rights Act. 

The Bureau coordinates employment security activities with other Government agencies and the public, and advises the legislative and executive branches on employment security matters. It plans programs on a nationwide basis. To facilitate sound program planning, it collects and analyzes operational and economic data, which in published form provide Government, labor, management, and the public with information of value in assessing economic trends and developments.

The Bureau conducts evaluations of the administration and operation of 

State employment security agencies. 

This involves the measurement of achievements, the making of recommendations for improving State administrative operations and management, and the provision of assistance in the establishment of improved methods of administration and operation. 

Fiscal responsibilities involve jus tification of appropriation requests before Congress, allocation of funds among States, establishment of standards for expenditures, auditing of State fiscal accounts and records, filing of exceptions on funds improperly expended, review of applicable State laws and their execution, and certification of such laws to permit the allocation of Federal funds for administrative costs.

The Bureau provides leadership to the State employment security agencies, involving responsibility to: (1) develop and interpret national policies and goals; (2) study program needs and administrative problems; (3) develop techniques, tools, and measures for improvement in administration and program content; (4) promote adoption of improvements in State legislation and administration; and (5) provide continuing technical assistance and interchange of experience and information.

The Bureau works closely with State agencies in the development and maintenance of a well-selected and trained staff.

The Bureau coordinates nationwide developmental projects designed to provide tools, methods, and material for adaptive use throughout the employment security system. From such coordinated efforts have come such products as the Dictionary of Occupa tional Titles, occupational tests, and occupational job descriptions.

The Bureau cooperates with other offices of the Department and with other Federal agencies in the war on poverty, especially in developing employability among culturally, educationally, and economically deprived youth. It is responsible under title VI of the Civil Rights Act for insuring that the Federal-State employment security program is administered without discrimination on the basis of race, color, or country of origin. 

The Bureau also actively participates in mobilization planning and in E the preparation being made by the Federal Government for national emergencies which might arise. In addition, the Bureau coordinates civil defense and mobilization activities in 

State employment security agencies. 

The Bureau's employment service program responsibilities, as assigned to its United States Employment Service under the provisions of the Wagner- Peyser Act, include assistance in establishing and maintaining a system of public employment offices in the States and territories; assistance in coordinating the system throughout the country and increasing its usefulness by developing and prescribing minimum standards of efficiency; collecting and furnishing information as to opportunities for employment and other information of value in operating a system, including information about labor area developments by industry and occupation and classification of areas according to relative labor supply; maintaining a public employment service for the District of Columbia, a veterans' service devoted to securing employment for veterans, and a placement service for agriculture and its workers; and maintaining a system for interarea recruitment of labor among the States. 

The United States Employment Serv ice guides and assists the States in placement functions, occupational analysis, counseling, and testing functions; in maximizing employment opportunities for veterans, older workers, youth, handicapped workers, members of minority groups, and workers affected by the impact of automation and changing technology; in promoting community efforts toward the greatest possible use of the labor force; in promoting use by employers of the public employment service; and in

providing materials and techniques to employers for effective use of man power. The Employment Service as sists State agencies in providing a full range of services to rural areas. In many States mobile teams of counselors, interviewers, and test administrators extend these services. 

The United States Employment 

Service has cooperative arrangements with Selective Service in counseling, testing, job developing, and training of educationally deficient rejectees. 

Through its Veterans Employment 

Service, it also has arrangements with the Department of Defense to assist in the employment reorientation of military retirees before and after retirement.

A new youth program will provide intensive job development, employment, and employment-related assistance to youth, especially the disadvantaged and school dropouts, through the establishment of 200 youth opportunity centers and the designation of additional youth specialists. Eligible youths will be referred to potential employers, the Job Corps, the Neighborhood

Youth Corps, and to training projects under the Manpower Development and Training Act.

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1952, the United States Employment Service, with the assistance of the State employment security. offices, reviews and makes determinations for guidance of the Attorney

General on requests for the importation and employment of alien workers. 

The Office of Farm Labor Service develops policies and procedures to provide a complete placement service to agricultural workers and employers. 

It directs and coordinates this service to insure that year-round and seasonal labor requirements of agriculture are met and that individual workers seeking employment in agriculture are exposed to all available job opportunities. 

It seeks to provide an orderly, expeditious, seasonal movement of migrant workers to successive jobs through interstate clearance and the Annual 

Worker Plan by maintaining current, reliable information regarding crop conditions and employment opportu nities. The Farm Labor Service is re sponsible for insuring that in the interstate recruitment of farmworkers applicable standards and the Secretary's regulations are met relating to housing, transportation, wages, and other conditions. It also provides for Federal registration of interstate farm labor contractors. The office reviews and makes determinations on request for the importation and employment of alien farmworkers under the Immigration and Nationality Act. It cooperates with other Federal agencies in determining the need for training in farm skills, recruiting of potential trainees, and placing of graduate trainees. 

Under the Area Redevelopment Act, the Federal-State employment service system obtains facts needed for determining eligibility of areas and reviews manpower aspects of overall economic plans for these areas. Under the Man power Development and Training Act, the Employment Service determines training needs, selects and refers trainees, develops job opportunities, refers trainees to jobs, follows up placement of trainees, and is responsible for planning and carrying out some pilot labor mobility demonstration projects to determine how effective relocation assistance can be in reducing unemploy ment. The Neighborhood Youth Corps 

(NYC) is responsible for administering the work-training program for unemployed young men and women, age 16 through 21, from low-income families, authorized in title I, part B, of the 

Economic Opportunity Act of 1964 (78 

Stat. 508; 42 U.S.C. 2701).

The purpose of this part of the antipoverty program is to make it possible for young people to remain in school, or return to school if they have already left; or to provide useful work experience to increase employability and to develop good work habits for those who are unemployed and out of school. 

Enrollees in the NYC undertake useful public service types of work which would not otherwise be performed in their own home community. Examples are the conservation, development, or management and improvement of State or community natural resources or recreational facilities, and a wide variety of assistance to teachers and ad- ד! A broad range of work is being undertaken, but the jobs are simple and almost invariably in the "helper" or "aide" category. NYC projects originate with local or State groups. 1965 and 1966.

The NYC operates through its Washington headquarters, and a field staff directed from seven regional offices. 

Functions of field representatives are to inform State and local authorities and private nonprofit agencies about the NYC, to assist in developing suitable projects, to review proposed projects and to follow their progress, and to report on needs of youth for work experience in their regions.

Assistant Secretary for Labor-Management Relations The Assistant Secretary for Labor- Management Relations has responsi bility for the Department's labor-management relations activities as well as the activities of the Wage and Hour and Public Contracts Divisions. He

serves as Administrator of the Labor- 

Management Services Administration. 

Labor-Management Services Administration The Labor-Management Services Administration was established by Sec retary's Order 24-63, dated August 8, 1963. The Labor-Management Serv ices Administrator is responsible for the direction and coordination of all the Department's labor-management relations programs and activities. He is assisted by a Deputy Administrator and other officials having responsibility for the specific functions of the comprehensive labor-management relations program. 

The Labor-Management Services 

Administration is composed of the offices described in the following paragraphs.

OFFICE OF LABOR-MANAGEMENT AND WELFARE-PENSION REPORTS.-The Of fice administers and enforces the provisions of the Welfare and Pension

Plans Disclosure Act (72 Stat. 997, as amended; 29 U.S.C. 301 note), and the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959 (73 Stat. 

519; 29 U.S.C. 401 note) for which the Secretary of Labor has authority and responsibility.

The Welfare and Pension Plans Dis closure Act provides for the reporting and disclosure of information concerning the operation of welfare and penhandling such plans, provides specific sion plans and the bonding of persons power to investigate complaints and to secure compliance and restrain violations of the law through civil judicial proceedings, and to issue binding and authoritative opinions and interpretations.

The Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act provides for the reporting and disclosure of certain financial transactions and administrative practices of labor organizations and employers; the prevention of abuses in these areas and in the administration of trusteeships by labor organizations; and the enforcement of standards and procedures with respect to the election and removal of officers of labor organizations.

Both acts authorize the conduct of investigations and the initiation of civil and criminal legal actions.

OFFICE OF LABOR-MANAGEMENT POLICY DEVELOPMENT.-This office, under the direction and supervision of a Director, serves as a focal point for the Department's policy planning, policy development, and research activities in the labor-management relations area. 

Policy planning and development responsibilities of this office include: review of the performance of collective bargaining and its contribution toward meeting current economic and social needs; development of objectives for

Federal programs affecting collective bargaining; development of policy for labor-management relations legislation and Executive orders; and study of private policies affecting collective bargaining to determine impact, contributions, or problems they may present in the labor-management relations field. 

In the area of research and analysis, responsibilities include: coordination of the labor-management relations research activities within the Department; assistance in arranging for data and analysis related to particular collective bargaining situations; analyses of the performance of collective bargaining in particular situations; development and execution of research programs related to the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act and the Welfare and Pension Plans 

Disclosure Act; and specialized studies of labor-management relations and collective bargaining.

OFFICE OF FEDERAL EMPLOYEE-MAN- AGEMENT RELATIONS.-The Director of this office administers the functions vested in the Secretary under section 

11 of Executive Order 10988 of January 17, 1962, which include: the ex amination and handling of agency or employee organization requests for the nomination of arbitrators in cases involving appropriateness of units for the purpose of exclusive recognition or questions as to majority status determinations, and in appropriate cases makes such nominations; and the rendering of such assistance as may be appropriate to Federal agencies in connection with advisory decisions or determinations.

The Office issues interpretations; develops and issues policies, procedures, and guides; recommends the issuance, revision, or amendment of rules and regulations; renders assistance and advice to agencies and employee organizations concerning the order and the Standards of Conduct for employee organizations and the Code of Fair Labor Practices; maintains liaison with the Civil Service Commission and other agencies and performs other advisory and technical services to implement the order.

Wage and Hour and Public Contracts Divisions 

[For regulations codified under this head ing, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 29, Chapter V; Title 41, Chapter 50] The Wage and Hour Division was established pursuant to the provisions 

1of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 

June 25, 1938 (52 Stat. 1060; 29

U.S.C. 201-219). The Public Con tracts Division was created to admin ister the Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act of June 30, 1936 (49 Stat. 

2036; 41 U.S.C. 35-45). The two Divisions were consolidated by order of the Secretary of Labor on August 21, 1942. The Wage and Hour and Public 

Contracts Divisions are headed by an Administrator, appointed by the President with the consent of the Senate. 

The Fair Labor Standards Act of 

1938, as amended, establishes, subject to specified exemptions, minimum wage, overtime compensation, and child labor standards for employees who, on an individual basis, are engaged in interstate or foreign commerce, including any closely related process or occupation directly essential thereto. The act also applies to any employee in an enterprise engaged in commerce or the production of goods for commerce, as defined in the law, including employees handling, selling, or otherwise working on goods that have been moved in or produced for commerce.

The Equal Pay Act of 1963, which amends the Fair Labor Standards Act, requires employers to pay equal wages within an establishment to men and women doing equal work on jobs requiring equal skill, effort, and respon-

The Walsh-Healey Public Contracts 

Act requires Federal Government supply contracts in amounts exceeding $10,000 to contain stipulations with respect to payment of minimum wages and overtime, nonemployment of child and convict labor, and observance of certain safety and health standards. 

WHPC's national office develops policies and programs, issues regulations and interpretations, conducts economic research, develops certification standards for learners, apprentices, full-time students, and handicapped workers, establishes prevailing minimum wage rates under the Public 

Contracts Act, coordinates the enforce ment program, and directs a continuous evaluation to assure uniform and proper application of the acts. 

WHPC operates through 11 regions, each headed by a regional director who is responsible for investigation and enforcement activities in his region. Field offices and field stations operate within each region. An area office is located in Puerto Rico. In addition, safety and health investiga tions under the Public Contracts Act are conducted under special agreement by State agencies in a number of 

States. 

WHPC's investigators gather data regarding wages, hours, and other conditions and practices of employment.

They investigate facts and practices necessary for the enforcement of the acts. 

To recover unpaid minimum and/ or overtime wages, the Administrator may supervise payment of back wages and, in certain circumstances, the 

Secretary of Labor may bring suit for back pay upon the written request of the employee. The Secretary of Labor may also obtain a court injunction to restrain an employer from violating the law, including the unlawful withholding of proper minimum wage and overtime compensation. 

Wage determination activities are conducted under the acts encompass ing: (1) the Public Contracts wage determination program; (2) the Fair

Labor Standards Act industry commit tee program applicable to Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, and American

Samoa; and (3) the special minimum wage programs authorized for learners, apprentices, full-time students, and handicapped workers.

Regulations and research activities encompass programs for preparing interpretations and rulings on the general provisions of the acts and on exemption problems, directing economic research on administrative and legislative matters, conducting studies on the economic effect of minimum wage and overtime provisions, and preparing and analyzing statistics of operations.

WHPC also disseminates information and provides guidance concerning its functions and practices and the responsibilities and rights of employers and employees under the acts. 

Assistant Secretary for International Affairs

The Assistant Secretary for Inter national Affairs has responsibility for the Department's international activities, and for the Bureau of International Labor Affairs. He serves as the 

U.S. Government member of the Gov erning Body of the International Labor Organization (ILO), as head of the 

U.S. delegation to the Annual Conference of the ILO, and as a member of the Board of Foreign Service. 

Bureau of International Labor Affairs 

The Bureau was established on December 31, 1959, replacing the Office of International Labor Affairs origi nally established in 1947.

Under the dew fore wi 3 and Sing The re

policy direction of the Assistant Secre tary of Labor for International Affairs, the Bureau is headed by an Administrator who is responsible for discharging Department of Labor functions in the international labor field. Under the policy direction of the Assistant Secre tary, the Administrator is also charged with mobilizing, directing, and coordinating all other international activities of the Department's various specialized offices and bureaus. 

These functions and responsibilities of the Bureau include advising on the implications of international labor developments in relation to U.S. foreign and domestic policy, analyzing the impact of domestic policy and developments on labor aspects of foreign affairs, recommending operations designed to promote the United States national interest in the foreign labor field generally and with respect to specific areas of the world, and, with the assistance of other offices and bureaus, operating programs affecting labor which are designed to implement foreign policy. 

The Bureau's staff of geographic area specialists develops detailed action programs in the field of labor for the various foreign countries. Through these country programs, the Government's efforts are coordinated to achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives as they relate to labor abroad.

The Department of Labor has pri mary responsibility, under the overall foreign policy guidance of the Department of State, for United States participation in the International Labor

Organization. 

The Bureau also carries out the Department's responsibilities for assisting the Department of State in the management of the Foreign Service, including the labor attaché and Foreign

Service labor-reporting programs (the 

Department has statutory membership on the Board of the Foreign Service); for representation on delegations and formulation of labor policy in connection with United States participation in the United Nations Economic and

Social Council and its various commissions; for participation in the 

Trade Staff Committee and other interagency trade expansion activities and for staff support for the Department's representatives on the Trade

Expansion Act Advisory Committee and the Trade Executive Committee; and for participation of labor missions in the Government's international trade fair program. In these activities the Bureau relies upon technical assistance from other bureaus of the Department.

The Bureau coordinates and directs programs, both its own and those of other bureaus, which are carried on by the Department under various acts of 

Congress and under administrative agreements with other agencies for development of a fund of labor and manpower knowledge for use both in domestic and overseas programs; for development of a reservoir of labor and manpower experts; and for programs of technical cooperation and exchange of persons. As requested, consultants are supplied for foreign assignments, technical materials are furnished for use abroad, and training programs are conducted in the United States for foreign nationals. These programs are implemented in cooperation with the Department's bureaus and regional offices, State departments of labor, American trade unions, management, and other private organizations.

The Bureau's responsibility for advice on the implications of international labor developments in relation to 

United States foreign and domestic policy calls for a continuing program of analysis of such labor developments and their economic and social implications in foreign countries. This program, as well as the other international programs of the Department, call for active and current research on foreign labor developments. In this connection, great reliance is placed upon the

Division of Foreign Labor Conditions of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, which is responsible for research on labor around the world.

Women's Bureau 

The Women's Bureau, first estab lished as the Woman-In-Industry Serv ice in 1918, and made permanent by act approved June 5, 1920 (41 Stat. 

987; 29 U.S.C. 11), is charged with formulating standards and policies for promoting the welfare of wage-earning women, improving their working conditions, increasing their efficiency, and advancing their opportunities for profitable employment. It investigates and publishes reports upon matters pertaining to the welfare of working women.

The Bureau is concerned with all women at work, or seeking work, and with their training and skills; with 

Boston, Mass.: women in all fields of employment; with the student selecting her career; with the girl on her first job and the older woman worker; and with women who are both homemakers and wage earners.

Continuous research is carried on by the Bureau's technical experts to help it formulate policies and programs. 

Some studies provide information on the trends in the employment of women and on the characteristics of the female work force. Such studies point up the changes taking place and their impact on women. Other studies are concerned with employment opportunities, wages, and conditions of work in individual occupations or industries. Problems relating to the dual role of women as workers and homemakers receive attention. Factors affecting the earnings or income of women workers, the financial responsibility of women for family support, and special needs of women workers are analyzed with a view to action programs where indicated.

The Bureau's director is appointed by the Secretary of Labor. Fifteen district offices administer one or more of the various compensation acts.

The Bureau determines all questions arising under the Federal Employees'

Compensation Act. (For provision for review of its decisions, see Employees'

Compensation Appeals Board.) The 

Bureau determines what employments come within the scope of the law, whether the injury for which compensation is claimed occurred while in the performance of duty, the period for which compensation may be paid, the amount thereof, and, in case of death,

the persons entitled to receive such compensation. The Bureau makes arrangements to provide prompt and competent medical and hospital services for employees injured in the Federal service, and payment of monetary benefits. 

1950, provided for the transfer of the Board and its functions to the Department of Labor.

The Board consists of three members appointed by the Secretary of Labor, one of whom is designated as chairman and administrative officer. It performs a quasi-judicial function in deciding appealed cases.

Under the Longshoremen's and 

Harbor Workers' Compensation Act, the Bureau authorizes insurance carriers to write insurance to secure the payment of compensation, authorizes employers to act as self-insurers, prepares opinions on questions of law for the guidance of deputy commissioners until such questions are finally settled by judicial determination, and supervises the defense of litigation arising out of this law. Decisions upon claims for compensation under this act, and local supervision of the enforcement of the act, are under deputy commissioners of the Bureau who have jurisdiction over districts. The decision of the deputy commissioner in respect to a claim for compensation is subject to review by Federal district courts on questions of law.

The Appeals Board was created for the purpose of reviewing and, subject to applicable law, making final decisions on appeals taken from determinations and awards with respect to employees of the Federal Government and of the District of Columbia (except members of the police and fire departments) in cases arising under the Federal Employees' Compen sation Act (5 U.S.C. 751). The right of appeal has been extended to employees of the Canal Zone Government and of the Panama Canal Company. 

Appeals may be taken to the Board on disputed questions of law and fact and on the basis of abuse or failure to exercise discretion. 

All compensation benefits authorized by this law are paid by the employer direct or through his authorized insurance carrier. The cost of administration of this law is paid from a 

Federal appropriation.

Bureau of Labor Statistics 

The Bureau of Labor, the predeces sor of the Bureau of Labor Statistics, was established in the Department of the Interior, by act of June 27, 1884.

In 1913, after several changes in status, it became the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the newly created Department of Labor. The Bureau is the Govern ment's principal factfinding agency in the field of labor economics, particularly with respect to the collection and analysis of data on employment and manpower, productivity and technological developments, wages, industrial relations, work injuries, prices, and costs and standards of living.

The Bureau has no enforcement or administrative functions. Practically all of the basic data it collects from workers, businessmen, and from other governmental agencies are supplied by voluntary cooperation based on their interest in and need for the analyses and summaries which result. The research and statistical projects planned by the Bureau grow out of the needs of these groups, as well as the needs of Congress and the Federal and State governments. The information collected is issued in special bulletins and in its official publication, the Monthly 

Labor Review. 

ECONOMIC GROWTH.-The Bureau performs research and coordinating functions in relation to the program of work on economic growth and employment opportunities, utilizing a wide range of data including the effects of trends in population, labor force, employment, productivity, factor payments and income distribution, prices, consumer expenditure patterns, foreign trade, etc., on various economic models and projections.

EMPLOYMENT AND THE LABOR 

FORCE.-Data are published each month on the labor force, employment, and unemployment, by age, sex, occupation, etc., based on a sample survey of the population. At recurring intervals the surveys provide estimates of the educational attainment of the dents, family relationship of workers, labor force, the employment of students, family relationship of workers, and other personal and economic characteristics of the labor force. 

National estimates are published each month on the employment of wage and salary workers in 365 manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries. National labor turnover rates are provided for 224 industries in manufacturing, mining, and communications. In cooperation with State agencies, comparable employment and labor turnover data are provided for all of the States and for larger metropolitan areas. Comprehensive analyses, together with all the Government's current statistics on labor force, employment, and unemployment are published monthly in Employment and Earnings.

The Bureau conducts studies of trends in unemployment, of problems affecting particular groups in the working population, such as youth and older workers, and prepares analyses and projections of the changing size and composition of the labor force. In addition, the Bureau is responsible for assessment of the military manpower pool and for projections of potential manpower resources, in relation to requirements under conditions of national emergency.

Exploratory research is now being undertaken looking toward the development of a national system of statistics on job vacancies. Such data will contribute greatly to the improvement of knowledge about the Nation's labor markets and will be useful in interpret-

ing trends in the levels of unemployment and the requirements for manpower development and retraining. 

Developmental research is being conducted in additional areas pursuant to the recommendations of the

President's Committee To Appraise 

Employment and Unemployment

Statistics. 

AVERAGE HOURS AND EARNINGS.- 

Gross average hourly and weekly earnings, and average weekly hours, for production or nonsupervisory workers, are issued currently by the Bureau for about 323 industries on a national basis. Average weekly overtime hours are published currently for 143 manufacturing industry groups. Through the cooperative State program, similar data are made available for all States and the more important metropolitan areas. These statistics are reported monthly in Employment and Earnings.

WAGES AND INDUSTRIAL RELA- 

TIONS. Occupational wage surveys are made annually in 80 major labor markets. These studies provide information on the level and distribution of wages and salaries for office clerical, professional and technical, maintenance and power plant, and custodial, warehousing, and shipping occupational categories. Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. A more comprehensive national survey of salaries for professional, administrative, technical, and clerical occupations is made annually.

YSIS. Reports are published on the long-range employment outlook in important occupations and industries. 

Data on employment trends, earnings, hours, industrial hazards, collective bargaining agreements, and technological trends collected by the Bureau are included for guidance purposes, together with information from other Government and private sources. Conclusions of these studies are published in the Occupational Outlook Quarterly, a periodical issued four times in the school year, and biennially in the 

Occupational Outlook Handbook. 

elect Occupational wage surveys are made in selected industries covering major manufacturing and nonmanufacturing industries over a 5-year cycle. A few industries are studied annually; most industries, however, are studied at 3to 5-year intervals. Information is provided on a national and regional basis and for selected areas of concentration. Work schedules and supplementary wage benefits are also summarized in these studies. Annual surveys are made in 68 cities of wage rates agreed upon in union contracts for a limited number of occupations in printing and publishing, local streetcar and bus operations, the building trades, and motor trucking. Quarterly data are available for 100 cities for seven selected occupations in the construction trades.

Plans are now being implemented to obtain current employment statistics by occupation, with the goal of developing a regular annual statistical series on employment in about 100 of the most important professional, technical, skilled, and clerical occupations. Such data are needed to refine estimates of future occupational requirements and opportunities, to evaluate the impact of automation and technological change and shift in demand on the occupational structure of the labor force, and to measure the effectiveness coust Distributions of production and related workers and of other nonsupervisory employees by straight-time average hourly earnings are periodically established in studies that provide national and regional estimates for manufacturing and selected nonmanufacturing industries for minimum wage legislation and other purposes. pr Bu ag 3 and Information on current trends in wage rates and wage practices is presented in a monthly report summarizing current wage settlements. In addition, statistical summaries are preothe ROD re

1 pared quarterly and annually. Chronologies showing the historical development of wage rate changes are presented for important bargaining situations in selected industries. A series of indexes of changes in wages and salaries for selected occupational groups are maintained. 

Studies of employer expenditures on selected fringe benefits and of the composition of payroll hours are made over a 3-year cycle in manufacturing and in selected nonmanufacturing industries.

The Bureau maintains a file of current union contracts and constitutions which is used as factual background material by unions, employers, and conciliation agencies in the settlement of industrial disputes, and as a guide to the preparation of new agreements.

The Bureau publishes analyses of union agreements in individual industries and agreement provisions concerning such subjects as arbitration and grievances, job security issues, and wage provisions. Similar studies of health, insurance, and pension plans, and other employee benefit plans and of the substantive provisions of union constitutions are also made. Current statistics on work stoppages resulting from industrial disputes are issued monthly with detailed analyses available annually. The Bureau publishes a biennial Directory of National and International Labor Unions in the

United States, and studies of union membership, structure, and procedures.

PRODUCTIVITY MEASUREMENT.-The 

Bureau publishes annual indexes of output per man-hour and unit manhour requirements for the private economy and broad industrial groupings such as manufacturing, mining, and agriculture. Annual indexes are published comparing trends in productivity with those of employment costs per hour, employment costs per unit of output, and prices for the total private and nonagricultural sector of the economy. Indexes are also prepared for selected industries in manufacturing and nonmanufacturing relating output to the man-hours of production workers and of all employees.

STUDIES IN TECHNOLOGY.-The 

Bureau conducts studies of technological developments and automation and their implications for productivity and manpower requirements. These studies explore the technological outlook among industries and the impact of major innovations across industry lines. 

These studies also deal with the adjustments made by plants introducing new kinds of equipment, including planning, training, and transfer of workers, the outlook for innovations and for technological developments in different industries, with the projected impact on productivity and changes in number and kind of workers who will be needed.

LABOR REQUIREMENTS.-Studies of the importance of construction in generating employment include estimates for direct, on-site construction activities and for indirect, off-site activities such as manufacturing, mining, and transportation. They also provide information on the kind of construction labor used, the timing of construction, and the kinds of materials used. 

INDUSTRIAL HAZARDS.-The Bureau conducts quarterly surveys on work injuries in manufacturing, and annual surveys in both manufacturing and nonmanufacturing in a large number of industries. National estimates are prepared annually for all disabling work injuries, by extent of disability for major industry groups. Special studies are made in industries with high accident rates, to determine accident causes and thereby to stimulate accident prevention programs in the industries studied.

Technical services are extended to State agencies to assist them in the development of better accident statistics. Currently, State-Federal cooperative injury rate surveys are conducted in 12 States.

PRICES AND LIVING CONDITIONS.- 

The Bureau is the principal agency of the Federal Government concerned with price statistics outside the field of agriculture. It is also responsible for conducting surveys of family expenditures and incomes, developing family budget studies, and analyzing changes in levels and standards of living. 

Studies of consumer expenditures and income are conducted from time to time. Such studies were made in 66 cities during 1961 and 1962, and in 5 cities in the spring of 1964. Standard budgets are developed at irregular intervals, the last being for 1959. 

The Bureau computes a Consumer 

Price Index for the Nation which is published monthly. Retail prices are collected regularly in 56 cities for food and for other items such as clothing, house furnishings, miscellaneous goods and services, and rents. In addition to a U.S. index, city indexes are published monthly for the 5 largest cities and quarterly for 18 other cities.

LABOR CONDITIONS IN OTHER COUN- 

TRIES.-Basic information and current developments in the labor field in other countries are covered in the Bureau's program. Discussions of the general labor situation in individual countries and summaries of available information on a particular subject in the field of labor economics throughout the world appear in the Monthly Labor

Review and in special reports published from time to time in foreign labor reports and bulletins. The Bureau also issues a monthly summary called Labor Developments Abroad. 

The Wholesale Price Index includes primary market prices of over 2,200 raw materials, semimanufactured goods, and manufactured goods, divided into 15 major groups, 85 subgroups, 288 product classes. These data are also classified into 34 indexes by stage of processing, 8 indexes by durability of product, and 27 other special purpose indexes. The Bureau maintains records of price quotations for over 7,000 series for goods sold in primary markets. Primary market price indexes are published weekly and monthly. In addition, it publishes a daily index of spot market prices.

The Solicitor of Labor 

The Solicitor has responsibility for all the legal activities of the Department, for the coordination and preparation of the Department's legislative proposals, reports and testimony on proposed legislation, including executive branch clearances, and for the administration of the Davis-Bacon and related acts except as specifically reserved to the Secretary. He serves as legal adviser to the Secretary and other officials of the Department.

Office of the Solicitor The Solicitor is the chief law officer of the Department of Labor. With the assistance of the Deputy Solicitor, he directs and supervises the legal work of the entire Department. Responsible to him is an immediate staff of assistants and attorneys in Washington and in the field offices of the Department throughout the United States and Puerto Rico. 

The Solicitor is also empowered to perform the duties of the Secretary of 

Labor in certain instances. Pursuant to delegation of authority from the Secre tary, he exercises final authority in the 

Department over the withdrawal of originals and copies of files, records, and documents of the Department, in determining the necessity of publishing documents in the Federal Register, and over tort claims arising out of the Department's activities; performs administrative and interpretative functions under the Davis-Bacon Act and related prevailing-wage statutes, the 

Copeland Act, the Contract Work Hours Standards Act, and the func tions of the Department under Reorga nization Plan 14 of 1950 and the stat utes listed in the Department's Regu lations, Part 5 (29 CFR Part 5), ex cept those functions that have been delegated to the Wage Appeals Board. 

Among the major Department activities serviced by the Solicitor are those relating to manpower, development and training and work training programs for youth under the poverty program, minimum wages and maximum hours, equal pay, child labor, employment security, adjustment assistance for workers, registration of farm labor contractors, veterans readjustment assistance program, workmen's compensation, veterans' reemployment rights, apprenticeship training, safety and health on Government contracts and of longshoremen, labormanagement laws, welfare and pension plans reporting and disclosure, and international labor affairs.

The Solicitor's Office interprets statutes administered or coordinated in the Department, drafts rules and regulations implementing such statutes, and furnishes legal services in connection with hearings and other administrative proceedings leading to formulation of rules and regulations implementing such statutes.

The Solicitor is in charge of the litigation of the Department. He represents the Secretary of Labor in the institution and prosecution of all civil court actions involving the Fair Labor Standards Act, including preparation of briefs and argument of appellate cases and interpreting, instituting, and conducting proceedings involving the

Equal Pay Act. His Office assists in the preparation, trial, and briefing of criminal cases under the Fair Labor Standards Act, and civil actions to recover damages under the Public Contracts Act, the Mexican labor program, and the Immigration Act; represents the Department officials in administrative hearings; and performs legal services in the preparation, institution and trial of enforcement cases in the Fed eral courts under the Labor-Management Reporting and Disclosure Act and Welfare and Pension Plans Dis closure Act;

Assistant Secretary for Administration 

The Assistant Secretary for Administration has responsibility for the Department's budgetary and fiscal ma tains the D mana cont Sel Service spa eni management, personnel management, administrative management, organization, the Library, and administrative ren aliz

services activities. He is assisted by the , who serves as the Department's Budget 

Officer and Comptroller, and the Assistant Assistant Secretary who serves as Director of Personnel. 

Office of the Assistant Secretary for

Administration The Office directs and coordinates all matters of administration and management in the Department and handles or supervises all contacts with 

Congress on budget matters. 

It reviews, evaluates, and approves proposed and existing programs to assure compliance with Department policies, plans, and budgetary directives; determines amounts and adequacy of presentation of budget estimates and apportionments. The 

Office develops, reviews, and approves organization structures within the several bureaus, and promulgates departmental regulations and procedures governing all budget, fiscal management, management analysis, and office service functions. It develops and maintains all major relationships outside the Department on administration and management matters and coordinates contacts with the Bureau of the

Budget, except those involving substantive legislation.

Services concerned with real property, space, communications, messenger service, central mail room facilities, parking space facilities, travel arrangements, local transportation facilities, procurement of articles and services, centralized duplicating and printing, and centralized stock and shipping rooms are provided by the Office on a departmentwide basis. Preparation of the budget for the Office of the Secretary and certain bureaus and offices and the provision of centralized accounting and payroll services are also responsibilities of the Office. 

Responsibility for the development and coordination of all plans and procedures necessary to provide management, fiscal, and administrative services for the execution of the mobilization and civil defense responsibility of the Department, including communications, establishing and maintaining relocation sites, safeguarding records and providing physical security measures, rests with the Office.

The Office directs and coordinates the personnel program of the Department and is responsible for the standards, procedures, and methods under which the program operates. It also directs management programs to improve employee-management relations, employee morale, employee training and utilization, and employee work performance appraisal and improvement.

LIBRARY.-The Library is a special ized collection of over 400,000 books, periodicals, and pamphlets on labor and related subjects. It provides reference service to the staff of the Department and to the public, circulates books and periodicals to the staff, and lends material to other libraries.

FRED H. Steininger. [For regulations codified under the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 41, Chapter 3; 

Title 45, Subtitle A] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Department of Health, Education, and 

Welfare was created by Reorganization 

Plan 1 of 1953. Under provisions of the act approved April 1, 1953 (67 

Stat. 18; 5 U. S. C. 623), the Plan became effective on April 11, 1953. The

Plan abolished the Federal Security 

Agency, created by Reorganization Plan I of 1939, and transferred all functions of the Federal Security Ad ministrator to the Secretary of Health,

Education, and Welfare and all components of the Agency to the Department.

PURPOSE.-The Department was established for the purpose of improving the administration of those agencies of the Government the major responsibilities of which are to promote the general welfare in the fields of health, education, and social security. 

ORGANIZATION.—The Department is administered under the supervision and direction of the Secretary. The structure of the Department is shown in the organization chart which appears on page 610.

Office of the Secretary SECRETARY.-The Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, as the head of an executive department, reports directly to the President, supervises and directs the Department, and carries out Federal responsibilities in relation to three federally aided cor porations: American Printing House for the Blind, Gallaudet College, and 

Howard University.

UNDER 

SECRETARY.-The Under 

Secretary serves as Acting Secretary in the absence of the Secretary and performs on behalf of the Secretary such functions and duties as the Secretary may designate. The Under 

Secretary has specific responsibility for coordinating field activities, overseeing the internal security program and the civil defense functions of the Department, directing the functions reserved to the Office of the Secretary under the Manpower Development and 

Training Act of 1962, and directing the functions reserved to the Office of the Secretary under the Grants for

Educational Television Broadcasting Facilities Act of 1962. He represents the Secretary in the Department's statutory relationships with American 

Printing House for the Blind, Gallaudet 

College, and Howard University.

OFFICE OF PUBLIC INFORMATION.- 

This Office is responsible for the gen-

eral direction and supervision of all public information activities of the 

Department. 

ASSISTANT SECRETARY (FOR LEGIS- LATION). The Assistant Secretary 

(for Legislation) serves as principal staff adviser to the Secretary in the coordination of the development and presentation of the Department's legislative program; serves as liaison with the Congress, external committees, commissions, organizations, or agencies dealing with legislative matters; and directs the Office of Program Analysis. 

ASSISTANT SECRETARY.-The Assist ant Secretary serves as principal staff adviser to the Secretary on departmentwide international programs and water supply and pollution control; and through the respective staff offices, coordinates the activities of the 

Department in these fields.

SPECIAL ASSISTANT TO THE SECRE- TARY (HEALTH AND MEDICAL AF- FAIRS). The Special  (Health and Medical Af fairs) reviews the health and medical programs of the Department and advises the Secretary with respect to the improvement of such programs and with respect to necessary legislation in health and medical fields. 

OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUN- SEL.-This Office renders legal advice and opinions on questions which arise in connection with administration and operation of programs and participates in the formulation of the Department's legislative program. 

OFFICE OF FIELD ADMINISTRATION.- The Director of Field Administration serves as principal adviser to the Secretary in the coordination of the field activities of the Department. The 

Office administers a program of assistance to the States in the administration of merit systems for personnel involved in grant-in-aid programs, and the statutory functions of the Secretary with respect to surplus property utilization.

OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATION.-The Assistant Secretary for Administration serves as principal adviser to the Secretary on administration; coordinates management responsibilities with program policies and operations. The 

Office performs all of the functions of the Secretary in the field of administrative and financial management; provides departmentwide coordination, leadership, and guidance on budgetary and financial management, personnel management, organization, administrative management, and administrative services.

Public Health Service 

Regulations, Title 42, Chapter I] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Public Health Service has its origin in an act of July 16, 1798 (ch. 77, 1 Stat. 

605), authorizing marine hospitals for the care of American merchant seamen. Subsequent legislation has vastly broadened the scope of its activities. 

The Public Health Service Act of July 1, 1944 (58 Stat. 682; 42 U. S. C. 

201), consolidated and revised substantially all existing legislation relating to the Public Health Service, including title VI of the Social Secu rity Act, and provided for greater assistance to States, for coordinated research, for establishment of a national tuberculosis control program, and for expansion of the commissioned corps. The basic Public Health Serv ice legal responsibilities have been broadened and expanded many times since 1944. 

Among the more important functions added have been those for the control and prevention of water pollution and air pollution; expanded fellowship and training programs; loans to students in the health professions; grants to States for planning comprehensive mental retardation programs; and the administration of construction grants for hospitals and medical facilities, waste treatment works, health research facilities, teaching facilities for health personnel, research centers and other facilities for the mentally retarded, and mental health centers.

PURPOSE.-The Public Health Serv ice, under the direction of the Surgeon

General, is the Federal agency specifi cally charged with responsibilities for protecting and improving the health of the people of the Nation. It is also responsible for collaborating with governments of other countries and with international organizations in world health activities. The major functions of the Service are: (1) to conduct and support research and training in the medical and related sciences, and in public health methods and administration; (2) to provide medical and hospital services to persons authorized to receive care from the Service, to aid in the development of the Nation's hospital and related facilities, and to prevent the introduction of communicable diseases into the United States and its possessions; and (3) to assist the

States and other governments in the application of new knowledge for the prevention and control of disease, the maintenance of a healthful environment, and the development of community health services.

ORGANIZATION.-The activities of the Service are organized into four bureaus: Office of the Surgeon Gen eral, Bureau of Medical Services,

Bureau of State Services, and National Institutes of Health; and the National Library of Medicine. 

The National Advisory Health 

Council and the advisory councils established for each major program area provide overall advice and policy guidance to the Surgeon General and review all research grant applications

in their area of competence. Advice and consultation is also secured from other advisory groups, from the Board of Regents of the National Library of 

Medicine, and from the Conference of 

State and Territorial Health Officers. 

In order to maintain direct contact with State and local authorities, with field offices of other Federal agencies, and with other official and nonofficial organizations concerned with its activities, the Service maintains a staff in the regional offices of the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare. 

These staffs are headed by regional health directors who represent the Surgeon General in interpreting and carrying out the broad policies of the 

Service. The regional health director is assisted by two associate regional health directors, one representing the programs of community health and the other, the programs of environmental health. The regional staffs work with. 

State authorities in developing and maintaining plans, programs, and budgets for Federal-State cooperative health programs.

Office of the Surgeon General The Office of the Surgeon General is a bureau composed mainly of staff services for the three operating bureaus and for the Surgeon General in his overall management of the organization. Its various divisions and offices assist in (1) studying the health needs of the Nation; (2) coordinating grant policies of the Service; (3) promoting the communication of scientific information; (4) providing overall program and policy direction to Service activities in the international health field and in the planning, negotiation, and administration of Service responsibilities for international health services with Federal agencies and international organizations; (5) directing and coordinating the Service's information, publications, and public inquiries programs; (6) developing general plans and programs under which personnel administration will be carried on within the Service; (7) managing budget and fiscal activities; (8) carrying out a comprehensive internal audit program; (9) providing for the management of all areas of general services; (10) facilitating organizational and procedural improvements and the general management of the Service; (11) supervising 

Public Health Service regional organizations and coordinating Public Health 

Service Federal-State activities; and (12) preparing the Nation to meet the health and water needs of the civilian population in the event of a national disaster.

THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR HEALTH STATISTICS.-The Center serves as the principal statistical arm of the Public Health Service and one of the major general purpose statistical organizations of the Government. This organization conducts continuing surveys and special studies of the Nation's population to determine the extent of illness and disability and to gather information related to these conditions. 

Areas of interest include the amounts and type of medical services received, the economic and social impact of illness and disability and methods of financing family health care. Such information establishes a current picture of the Nation's health and serves as a basis for predicting health trends.

The Center is also the principal instrument of Federal Government cooperation with the States in the collection of vital statistics (births, deaths, marriages, and divorces) and is the only source of national tabulation and analysis of such data. The Center also sponsors cooperative studies in foreign countries which provide useful comparative statistical data. 

Bureau of Medical Services 

The Bureau of Medical Services is the medical arm of the Public Health Service primarily concerned with developing and directing certain medical care and health services programs, and la sa كة ic

preventing the introduction of disease and the entry of mentally and physically defective aliens into the United 

States. 

Medical care is provided eligible beneficiaries through a system of Pub lic Health Service hospitals, outpatient clinics, and offices located throughout the United States where seamen employed on vessels of U.S. Registry, Coast Guard and other uniformed services personnel, and other legal beneficiaries receive hospitalization, medical and dental care, and preventive health services. In addition, dependents of uniformed services personnel are entitled to medical care and emergency dental care at such hospitals and outpatient clinics. A program of therapeutic and preventive health services, including a joint par ticipative Tribal-Public Health Service sanitation facilities construction activity, is provided for Indians and Alaska natives of the United States through area and field offices operating PHS 

Indian and Alaska native hospitals, health centers, school health centers, practical nurse training schools, and health stations; and through contracts with local governmental and nongovernmental resources. By direction of the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare, administrative supervision is provided Freedmen's Hospital in the District of Columbia. This is a general hospital for the treatment of acute medical and surgical conditions, with an extensive system of specialized clinices for outpatients. The hospital provides internship and clinical experience for medical students and graduates of 

Howard University. [For regulations codified under Freed men's Hospital, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 42, Chapter IV] 

Public laws and regulations to prevent the introduction of quarantinable and other dangerous communicable diseases into the United States are implemented through a system of worldwide epidemiological vigilance and in- =spection of arriving persons, animals, and things at ports and airports involved in international traffic. The medical provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act to exclude persons who present a danger to public health or a probability of an economic burden to public funds are implemented by medical examinations of aliens performed abroad, and by medical inspections at ports of arrival. 

Technical advice and personnel are furnished to assist other Federal agencies in health care programs for their employees and beneficiaries. Professional supervision and consultation are provided Service personnel directing medical care programs and/or performing medical services for certain other Federal agencies. Presently, personnel of the Public Health Service, assigned to this Bureau, administer medical care programs for other Fed eral agencies as follows: by law-Bureau of Prisons and the U.S. Coast 

Guard;

by interagency agreement- 

Bureau of Employees' Compensation in the Department of Labor. 

Bureau of State Services The Bureau of State Services is the principal operating bureau of the Service for Federal-State and interstate health programs. It gives general direction to activities in the two broad areas of Community Health and Environ mental Health designed to aid the States and communities in developing, establishing, and maintaining effective programs for the prevention, treatment, and control of diseases and for the prevention or control of environmental health hazards.

Within these areas, the Bureau conducts research; provides training; furnishes consultation and technical assistance to States and localities; conducts field surveys, investigations, and demonstrations; provides emergency disaster and epidemic aid to 

States; enforces corrective measures under certain statutes; conducts public information and education pro-

grams; and administers various grant and student loan programs. 

COMMUNITY HEALTH.-Bureau pro grams in this area are concerned with: (1) development of techniques for application of scientific observations in the fields of biology and medicine; (2) social, economic, and behavorial aspects of major health problems; (3) organization and delivery of coordinated systems of comprehensive health services, including health services for domestic migratory agricultural workers and their families; (4) development and effective utilization of professional, technical, and auxiliary health manpower; (5) training of professional health personnel, including loans for students in medical, dental, nursing, and related health professional schools; (6) planning and construction of hospitals and related medical facilities, including facilities for the mentally retarded, appropriate to needs of communities; and (7) construction of teaching facilities for medical, dental, nursing, and other health personnel. These programs include control of chronic diseases such as heart disease, cancer, diabetes, and arthritis; control of communicable diseases, including tuberculosis and veneral diseases; eradication of certain disease vectors; prevention and control of injuries; conservation of sight, hearing, and speech and control of mental retardation and other neurological neurological disorders; development and coordination of community health programs to remedy and alleviate problems of the chronically ill and aged; provision of consultation on nursing home and noninstitutional care services; administration of health programs in the fields of nursing services and resources; support and conduct of research, experiments, and demonstrations relating to the development, utilization, and coordination of services, facilities, and resources of hospitals, and other medical facilities. 

ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH.-Bureau programs in this area are concerned with: (1) the conduct and support of research to determine the nature, methods for effective measurement, and the health effects of environmental contaminants, including the total or cumulative effect as well as the individual effects on man; (2) the development of techniques and methods for practical control programs and for the maintenance of a healthful environment; (3) the study of political, social, and economic factors related to urbanization and metropolitan complexes as they affect environmental health, in order to develop effective methods of organization and administration in this field; (4) the development and effective utilization of professional and technical manpower and other resources for the broad field of environmental health; and (5) the administration of interstate quarantine regulations, and air and water pollution control enforcement measures. 

These programs include air pollution control; water supply and water pollution control; milk, food, shellfish, interstate and community sanitation; occupational health; radiological health; research and training in environmental health sciences; and arctic health; with research centers at Cincinnati, Ohio, and Anchorage, Alaska, and two new centers planned for North Carolina. and West Virginia, as well as specialized operational activities at numerous field stations located throughout the country.

National Institutes of Health The National Institutes of Health, the principal research arm of the Public Health Service, is primarily concerned with the extension of basic knowledge regarding the health problems of man and how to cope with them.

Fundamental laboratory and clini cal research in causes, prevention, and methods of diagnosis and treatment. of cancer, cardiovascular and geriatric diseases, allergy and infectious dissh ad

Ieases, arthritis and metabolic diseases, dental diseases and conditions, mental illnesses, and neurological and sensory diseases, is conducted by the National 

Cancer Institute, National Heart Institute, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National In stitute of Arthritis and Metabolic Dis eases, National Institute of Dental Re search, National Institute of Mental 

Health, and National Institute of Neurological Diseases and Blindness, re spectively. Patient facilities which service the clinical investigations programs of the Institutes are provided by the Clinical Center. 

In addition to conducting laboratory and clinical research programs, the Na tional Institute of Mental Health ad ministers programs of demonstrations and technical services to States and communities, generalized training of mental health and related personnel, and grants-in-aid for community mental health centers.

The NIH also initiates collaborative research programs which link its resources with the scientists in universities, hospitals, and industry, in pursuit of common research objectives. 

Grants-in-aid to public and nonprofit institutions and to individualsincluding research, training, and field investigations grants-in the general medical and health related sciences, and in maternal and child health and the basic sciences relating to the process of human growth are provided by the National Institute of General 

Medical Sciences and the National 

Institute of Child Health and Human 

Development, respectively, and by the other Institutes in the categorical areas of their interest. Fellowships are provided to individuals by the same organizational units.

The Division of Research Grants is responsible for coordinating and providing central administrative support to a major portion of the Public Health Service research grant and research training award programs.

The Division of Research Facilities and Resources makes grants-in-aid for health research facilities construction, and other across-the-board institutional grant programs for primate centers, general clinical research centers, special resources centers, and general research support. 

The Division of Biologics Standards administers the provisions of the Public Health Service Act that require the licensing of establishments and specified biological products when they are intended for sale, barter, or exchange in interstate commerce, or for export from or import into the 

United States. 

The Division of Research Services provides facilities, equipment, and a wide variety of scientific, technical, and supportive services essential to the needs of the medical investigator and research administrator at the National 

Institutes of Health. 

The Division of Computer Research and Technology conducts research and development programs in mathematics and other computer related sciences, in support of the National Institutes of Health's programs, and provides data processing for the National Insti tutes of Health. 

The Office of International Re search coordinates the National Institutes of Health's responsibilities in international medical research. 

National Library of Medicine The National Library of Medicine assists the advancement of medicine and related sciences through the collection, dissemination, and exchange of the world's biomedical literature. Holdings of the Library comprise the greatest collection of medical literature in the world. Bibliographic access to its collections is provided through 

MEDLARS, a computerized informa tion storage and retrieval system, and through the publication of guides in the form of catalogs, indexes, and bib-

liographies. Physical access to to the literature is provided through interlibrary loans, photoduplication, and reference services. The Library sup ports the translation and publication of biomedical literature and administers a program for the support of medical library development.

Office of Education 

(400 Maryland Avenue NW., Washington, D.C., 20202)  

Regulations, Title 45, Chapter I] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

Office of Education was created by act of March 2, 1867 (14 Stat. 434; 20

U.S.C. 1). In 1869 the Office of Edu cation became a part of the Department of the Interior; it was transferred to the Federal Security Agency upon that Agency's creation in 1939; and it became a constituent agency of the De partment of Health, Education, and 

Welfare upon the establishment of that 

Department in 1953.

PURPOSE. The statutory functions of the Office of Education are to collect such statistics and facts as shall show the condition and progress of education, to diffuse such information as shall aid the people of the United States in the establishment and maintenance of efficient school systems, and otherwise to promote the cause of edu cation. Subsequent acts and Executive orders have added related functions, including responsibilities for Federal financial assistance to education and for special studies and programs. 

ORGANIZATION.-The Office of Ed ucation includes the Office of the Commissioner and five operating bureaus: 

the National Center for Educational Statistics, the Bureau of Educational Research and Development, the Bu reau of International Education, the

Bureau of Educational Assistance Pro grams, and the Bureau of Higher Education. 

Office of the Commissioner The Office of the Commissioner is composed of the immediate Office of the Commissioner, four staff offices, and three program offices. 

STAFF OFFICES The Office of Administration pro vides budget, fiscal, personnel, and other administrative services for the

Office. 

The Office of Legislation plans, develops, and prepares new legislation necessary to carry out the functions and objectives proposed for the Office and analyzes and coordinates the preparation of congressional and other reports on all bills relating to education. 

The Office of Information directs the overall program of information and publications for the Office. It prepares news stories, magazine articles, statements, messages, and editorial research reports for the various media. It also provides technical and professional services for all publications of the Office.

The Office of Field Services coordi nates the field services performed by the various program staffs of the Office. It also discharges civil defense functions assigned to the Office. 

PROGRAM OFFICES The Office of Federal Education 

Activities provides staff services for the 

Federal Interagency Committee on Ed ucation. It identifies educational problems of national concern and recommends office activity or proposed policy. It develops full information on 

Federal activities that affect the Nation's educational well-being; designs surveys to measure the impact of Federal programs on education; and formulates recommendations in cases in which inconsistencies appear in such programs. In addition, it makes continuing evaluations of manpower de- 10分

velopment and utilization programs and recommends improvements in connection with these programs. 

The Office of Equal Educational 

Opportunity brings about compliance with the requirement that all recipients of Office of Education program funds assure the Office that such funds will be used without discrimination on the grounds of race, color, or national origin. Further, it is responsible for the conduct of a nationwide survey on the

I lack of availability of equal educational opportunities by reason of race, color, or national origin in public educational institutions at all levels in the United States. It provides technical assistance to school districts or State education agencies in the preparation, adoption, and implementation of plans for the desegregation of public schools. 

It also administers grants to school districts to support inservice training for school personnel in dealing with problems incident to desegregation and to employ specialists to advise on such problems. In addition, it arranges with colleges and universities for the operation of institutes designed to help elementary and secondary school personnel deal with problems encountered in desegregated schools.

Programs for Education of the Dis advantaged coordinates Office of

National Center for Educational Statistics The National Center for Educa tional Statistics, composed of the Office of the Assistant Commissioner and four divisions, is responsible for developing the statistical program for the Office of Education, and coordinating the information gathering activities for all programs. 

The Division of Data Sources and Standards maintains communications with all sources of educational statistics and provides leadership in development of standard terminology and reporting procedures. It aids States, local school districts, and institutions of higher education in development of data processing and reporting systems. 

In addition, it provides grants to State departments of education to improve and strengthen their educational information and statistical services.

The Division of Statistical Services provides technical assistance in all survey and other research activities conducted by the Office of Education. 

Its services include questionnaire design, computer programing and other data processing activities, and review of manuscripts for statistical accuracy. 

The Division of Statistical Analysis collects, analyzes, and disseminates statistics on education at all levels. It devises sampling plans for all Office of Education surveys and performs validity and methodological studies to improve techniques for collecting and analyzing statistical information. It also furnishes reference, estimate, and projection services for all aspects of educational statistical information. 

The Division of Operations Analysis is responsible for developing and maintaining a quantitative analytical model of the educational enterprise by integrating statistical information into a comprehensive structure, the principal function of which is to aid in appraising probable outcomes of significant policy or operational changes in American education. In addition, it analyzes the role of education in the life of the Nation insofar as this can be done in quantitative terms.

Social Security Administration 

 Reg ulations, Title 20, Chapter III] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Social Security Administration, under a Commissioner for Social Security, was established by the Federal Security Administrator pursuant to Reorgani zation Plan II, effective July 16, 1946, which abolished the Social Security Board (see appendix A) and transferred its functions, along with functions of the Children's Bureau, to the 

Federal Security Administrator. Dele gated to the Commissioner for Social Security were functions in connection with old-age and survivors insurance, unemployment insurance, and public assistance, and most maternal and child welfare programs. Other duties have subsequently been delegated to or transferred from the Administration by law or Presidential order.

The position of Commissioner for Social Security was reestablished as 

Commissioner of Social Security in the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare by Reorganization Plan 1, effective April 11, 1953. The Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare on 

January 28, 1963, reorganized the 

Social Security Administration, estab lishing the old-age, survivors and dis ability insurance (OASDI) and Fed eral credit union programs as the pri mary missions of the Administration. 

The Bureau of Old-Age and Survivors 

Insurance was abolished as a bureau and the Bureau of Family Services and the Children's Bureau were transferred to a new Welfare Administration.

It is responsible for studying problems of poverty and insecurity and the contributions that can be made to their solution by social insurance and related programs and for making recommendations for the most effective methods of improving social and economic security through social insurance. 

PURPOSE. The Social Security Ad ministration administers the Federal old-age, survivors and disability insur ance programs (title II of the Social 

Security Act, as amended, and title The purpose of old-age, survivors and disability insurance (OASDI) is to provide continuing income for individuals and their families as partial replacement of earnings lost through old-age or disability retirement or death. The OASDI program provides for the coverage of almost all persons engaged in gainful employment, including the military, the major exceptions being Federal civilian employees under a retirement system; selfemployed doctors of medicine; and domestics, agricultural workers, and self-employed persons having very low earnings. Entitlement to benefits is determined from the insured status of the individual; the age and relationship of the individual and his dependents; the application for such benefits; and in the case of disability benefits, the extent and expected duration of disability. Benefits are payable monthly in amounts related to the average monthly earnings of the insured person. A lump sum death benefit is payable under certain conditions. 

The Federal credit union program promotes thrift by encouraging cooperative, systematic saving and by making credit available in the short-term, EN AST AC Fe ce AS

small loan field at reasonable rates of interest, for credit union members. To accomplish these purposes, Federal credit unions provide convenient facilities for encouraging the development of habits of consistent regular saving out of current earnings.
