Regulations, Title 18, Chapter II] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The Tennessee Valley Authority is a cor poration created by act of Congress 

May 18, 1933 (48 Stat. 58; 16 U. Š. C. 

831-831dd). The statute provides for the development of the Tennessee River and its tributaries in the interest 

¹ Organization chart on page 634. 2 of navigation, the control of floods, and the generation and disposition of hydroelectric power. It also directs the corporation to operate the chemical facilities at Muscle Shoals, Ala., built during World War I, to develop new types of fertilizer in the interests of im- Other offices: Muscle Shoals, Ala., and Chattanooga, Tenn. 502

TENNESSEE VALLEY AUTHORITY 

503 יד 

FOX 

proved agriculture as well as of na tional defense. Executive Order 6161, of June 8, 1933, which implements sections 22 and 23 of the Tennessee Valley Authority Act, confers upon the corporation the authority to conduct investigations upon which additional legislation may be predicated in order to aid further the proper conservation, development, and use of the resources of the region. In the conduct of its operations and investigations, the corporation is authorized to cooperate with other national, State, and local agencies and institutions so that the fullest measure of effectiveness can be achieved. 

Nonpower functions of the corporation are financed from appropriations, and fertilizer-agriculture operations use in addition funds derived from the sale of fertilizer. Power operations are financed from power earnings. Capital for investment in power generating and transmission facilities, once derived primarily from appropriations, now is obtained through the issuance of the corporation's electric power bonds. 

Under the Government Corporation Control Act, the Comptroller General of the United States makes an annual commercial type audit of the corporation's accounts; the corporation may also arrange for audits of its accounts by certified public accounting firms. 

The corporation may sue or be sued in its corporate name, make contracts, purchase or lease real and personal property, and exercise the right of eminent domain in the furtherance of its statutory objectives. Title to real property must be taken in the name of the 

United States. 

PURPOSE.-Efforts to improve the 

Tennessee River system for navigation, dating from the administration of President Monroe in 1824, culminated in the statute creating the Tennessee Valley Authority, which imposes upon that agency the duty of bringing about an adequate and complete development of the river system through the construction of a series of dams upon the main stream and its principal tributaries. The relationship of the serious flood problem on the Tennessee River to that of the Mississippi was such that Congress directed the corporation to provide its projects with flood-control storage to alleviate these conditions. Along with its water resource development, agricultural and forestry programs are undertaken for both watershed protection and to improve the use of land resources for economic growth. 

ORGANIZATION 

The Board of Directors, appointed by the President with the approval of the Senate, is authorized by the Tennessee Valley Authority Act to exercise all powers of the corporation. It establishes general policies and programs, appraises progress and results, approves items of major importance, and establishes the basic organization. 

The General Counsel advises the 

Board on legal matters and is secretary to the corporation.

The General Manager is the principal TVA administrative officer. He directs and coordinates execution of programs, policies, and decisions of the Board of Directors, subject to such controls as it establishes. He assigns duties and makes delegations to divisions and approves major personnel appointments, organization changes, and management methods. He brings before the Board matters it should consider or approve.

The Office of the General Manager includes the Budget Staff, Government Relations and Economics Staff, Information Office, and the Washing ton Office. 

The Division of Law handles all legal problems in connection with the business of TVA.

The Division of Personnel admin isters policies and standards in personnel administration; the Division of 

Finance, in accounting, auditing, and

custody of TVA funds and property; the Division of Purchasing, in acquisition, transfer, shipping, and disposal of personal property; and the Division of 

Property and Supply, in acquisition, transfer, and disposal of real property and provision of computing, transportation, and office services.

The Division of Water Control Plan ning carries out plans for flood control and for multipurpose river system regulation. It also studies local flood problems and assists State and local governments and groups on measures to control or diminish the effect of such local conditions.

The Division of Navigation Devel opment formulates plans for the navigation engineering development of the Tennessee River system and for encouraging full and effective navigation use of the waterway in development of the region. 

The Office of Engineering Design and Construction designs and builds the dams, steamplants, and other permanent structures and engineering works required by TVA to carry out its objectives.

The Office of Power operates the TVA power system and executes engineering and other programs relating to the generation, transmission, and utilization of electric power. 

The Office of Agricultural and 

Chemical Development carries out programs for research and development in fertilizers and fertilizer manufacturing processes and for testing and demonstrating fertilizer value and use as an aid in soil and water conservation and in improved use of agricultural and related resources. It operates facilities to serve as a national laboratory in development of new and improved fertilizers and processes and in production of basic chemical materials in the munitions field essential to national defense. It aids in readjustment of agricultural areas affected by TVA operations; and carries out other activities related to management and use of agricultural resources and to national defense.

The Office of Tributary Area De velopment administers TVA's interests in comprehensive activities for obtaining maximum economic progress in tributary areas of the Tennessee Valley region. It helps local governmental bodies and citizen groups to organize and carry out unified resource development programs in each such area.

The Division of Forestry Develop ment conducts investigative and development programs in forestry, fish and game, and watershed protection.

The Division of Health and Safety carries out plans and policies on the health and safety of employees and of the public affected by TVA activities. and cooperates with other agencies in health and safety studies, demonstrations, and services.

The Division of Reservoir Proper ties manages reservoir properties and employee housing and services for construction projects, including property protection, law enforcement, and reception of public visitors. It is responsible for site planning and TVA's interests in recreation. It coordinates 

TVA's nonmilitary defense measures. 

The Land Between the Lakes Proj ect is a national outdoor recreation and conservation education demonstration area under development by TVA in the western portion of the Valley area. 

All personnel actions in TVA are based on merit and efficiency under the merit system authorized by the 

Tennessee Valley Authority Act and developed by TVA. The TVA has formal agreements with unions representing its employees. They cover matters suitable for collective bargaining and procedures to aid efficiency through employee-management cooperation. Management and employees jointly administer TVA's independent retirement system. As of January 1, 1965, TVA's employees numbered 16,500.

TENNESSEE VALLEY AUTHORITY 

505 

ACTIVITIES AREA OF OPERATION.-The natural course of the Tennessee River traverses a distance of about 650 miles from 

Knoxville, Tenn., to Paducah, Ky., where it empties into the Ohio River. 

It has six principal tributaries which drain the highest mass of mountains east of the Rockies in an area of the highest annual rainfall in the United =States, excepting the Pacific Northwest. The Tennessee basin includes parts of seven States, having an area of approximately 41,000 square miles; 

Valley counties had a 1960 population of about 3,662,900, about one-fifth of which lived on farms. 

NAVIGATION AND FLOOD CONTROL.- 

To out its mandate to provide a carry navigable channel in the Tennessee

River, to obtain a maximum of flood control in the drainage areas of the 

Tennessee, lower Ohio, and Mississippi

Rivers, and to generate hydroelectric power, TVA has constructed and maintained dams in the Tennessee River and in some of the larger tributaries.

The system of dams provides a 

9-foot navigable channel from the mouth of the river near Paducah, Ky., to Knoxville, Tenn. The system provides about 12,000,000 acre-feet of flood storage.

ELECTRIC POWER.-Under the stat ute, TVA is charged with the sale of power in such a way as to promote the widest possible use of electricity and assist in the economic development of the region. The statute prescribed that preference be given to municipalities and cooperative associations in the disposition of power. Power is sold directly to a number of industries whose use of power is large or otherwise unusual. 

As of January 1, 1964, the corporation had contracts for sale of power at wholesale with 106 municipalities, 50 cooperatives, and 2 privately owned utility companies, which distribute which distribute power to over 1,800,000 ultimate consumers under retail rates agreed upon with TVA. The corporation 743-116°-65 -33 had contracts for bulk sales of firm and interruptible power with about 35 large industrial concerns. It is also providing power to a number of projects, plants, and bases of Federal agencies. 

TVA also had contracts for purchase, sale, or interchange of power with a number of additional private power companies.

During the fiscal year 1964 TVA's power sales were 68.5 billion kw.hrs. and its gross revenues from the sale of power were $286.4 million.

The corporation's power-producing system had an installed capacity of 

14,175,615 kilowatts as of January 

1, 1965. This includes 15 hydroelectric plants in the Tennessee Valley, owned by the Aluminum Company of America, having a total installed capacity of 423,715 kilowatts; TVA directs water releases from Alcoa dams. 

It also includes power from five U.S. 

Corps of Engineers dams in the Cumberland Valley. TVA operates ten large steamplants, one small one, and has one major plant under construction.

FERTILIZER DEVELOPMENT. 

- The corporation is authorized to employ the properties at Muscle Shoals in order to develop improved fertilizers and better processes for their manufacture, in order to lower their cost to farmers in the interest of agriculture and the prevention of soil erosion. New types of plant food so developed are tested under conditions of scientific control primarily through the State land-grant colleges. The use of products produced by the corporation has been incorporated in the agricultural programs of established agencies, and because it involves readjustment in systems of agriculture in the interest of soil conservation, it provides a substantial measure of watershed protection in connection with the corporation's program. Emphasis is placed upon developing high analysis fertilizers.

DISTRIBUTION OF FERTILIZER MATE- 

RIALS.-TVA fertilizers are distributed for use only in research and educa-

tional programs. Most of the fertilizer produced by TVA is distributed for farm test-demonstrations supervised by the State agricultural extension services and distributor demonstrations conducted by selected farmer cooperatives and private wholesale fertilizer distributors. In each State the educational programs are jointly jointly planned by the land-grant colleges, the distributors, USDA agencies, and

TVA. 

Various TVA fertilizers have been tested by experiment stations in nearly all 50 States. Currently stations in 14

States are cooperating with TVA in research projects on fertilizer evaluation and use.

NATIONAL DEFENSE.-The TVA fer tilizer research and production facilities serve the national defense agencies in both peacetime and periods of national emergency. In national emergencies, national defense requirements have first call on TVA's technical staff and its research and production facilities. 

TVA is a principal source of electric power for several types of defense production, including the Atomic Energy Commission projects at Oak Ridge, Tenn., and Paducah, Ky., the Arnold 

Engineering Development Center at 

Tullahoma, Tenn., and the George C.

Marshall Space Flight Center, Hunts ville, Ala.

Approved. 

AUBREY J. WAGNER, Chairman, Board of Directors.

AND AUTHORITY.-The United States Arms Control and Dis armament Agency was established by the act approved September 26, 1961 (75 Stat. 631; 22 U.S.C. 2551).

PURPOSE. The Agency is respon sible for the conduct, support, and coordination of research for arms control and disarmament policy formulation; the preparation for and manage-

ment of United States participation in international negotiations in the arms control and disarmament field; the dissemination and coordination of public information concerning arms control and disarmament; and the preparation for, operation of, or, as appropriate, direction of United States participation in such international control systems as may under treaty arrangements become part of United States arms control and disarmament activities.

ORGANIZATION.-The Agency is headed by a Director, appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, who is responsible for the executive direction of the Agency. 

He also functions as the principal adviser to the President and the Secretary of State on arms control and disarmament matters and, under the direction of the Secretary, has primary responsibility within the Government for such matters. The Deputy Director, simi larly appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate, performs such duties and exercises such powers as the Director may prescribe and acts for and exercises the power of the Director during his absence.

The Agency's program responsibilities are primarily discharged through four bureaus-International Relations 

Bureau, Weapons Evaluation and

Control Bureau, Science and Technology Bureau, and Economics Bu reau-each of which is headed by an Assistant Director appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate. Staff elements participating in the policy formulation process are the Disarmament Advisory Staff and the Office of the General 

Counsel. Other organizational units with staff responsibilities are the Office of the Public Affairs Adviser, the Ex ecutive Staff, and the Reference Research Staff.

A General Advisory Committee of 

15 members, appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, meets at least twice each year to advise the President, the

Secretary of State, and the Director of the Agency on matters affecting arms control, disarmament, and world peace.

ACTIVITIES. A major share of the 

Agency's efforts has gone into nuclear test ban and comprehensive disarmament discussions and negotiations both at the United Nations and at Geneva.

Research occupies an important role, since the Agency is responsible for insuring the conduct of research into the manifold problems of arms control and disarmament through (1) studies performed with its own resources; (2) arrangements, including contracts, agreements, and grants, for the conduct of research, development, and other studies by private or public institutions or persons; and (3) coordination of activities conducted in this field by or for other Government agencies in accordance with procedures established by the organic law. 

Approved. 

WILLIAM C. Foster, Director.

Regulations, Title 5, Chapter I] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The United States Civil Service Commis sion was created by an act of Congress approved January 16, 1883 (22 Stat. 

403; 5 U.S.C. 632 et seq.; 40 U.S.C. 

42). An act of March 3, 1871 (16 

Stat. 514; 5 U.S.C. 631), had previously authorized the President to prescribe regulations for the admission of persons into the civil service. The 

Commission's authority was later broadened by legislation and Execu tive order. Reorganization Plan 5 of 

1949 provided for the designation of a Chairman and prescribed the functions of the Chairman and the 

Commissioners. 

PURPOSE. The fundamental pur pose of the law was to establish, in the parts of the service covered by its provisions, a merit system whereby selection for appointment should be made upon the basis of demonstrated relative fitness without regard to religious or political considerations, but the protection afforded by the principle of political nondiscrimination does not extend to membership in political parties or organizations which advocate the overthrow of our constitutional form of government; membership in such political parties or organizations constitutes by law a disqualification for Government employment. 

ORGANIZATION THE COMMISSION.-The Commis sion is composed of three members, not more than two of whom may be adherents of the same political party, who serve 6-year staggered terms. 

One member is designated by the

President of the United States to be the Chairman, and he is the chief executive and administrative officer of the organization. Another member is designated by the President as Vice

Chairman. 

THE OFFICE OF EXECUTIVE ASSISTANT TO COMMISSIONERS.-This office maintains control records of all matters submitted to the Commission for action, arranges meetings for the Commission, advises Members of Congress and others on civil-service matters, and compiles and records official minutes. of the Commission.

OFFICE OF THE EXECUTIVE DIREC- TOR.-The Executive Director, who is appointed by the Chairman, coordi-

נה nates the internal management of the Commission, directs the operating and staff activities of the Commission, and provides leadership in personnel administration through the Interagency

Advisory Group, which is composed of personnel directors of Federal agencies.

OFFICES AND BOARDS OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNSEL.- 

Advises the Commission on legal matters (including retirement); enforces political activity restrictions of the 

Hatch Act; drafts legislation; reviews proposed regulations and reports on pending legislation; cooperates with the Department of Justice in preparation of pleadings in and defense of court cases; receives and, when necessary, refers to the Federal Trade Commission, complaints about so-called civil-service schools; participates in preparation of material for the Federal 

Register; prepares requests for decisions from the Comptroller General and opinions of the Attorney General; and adjudicates tort claims filed against the Commission.

BOARD OF APPEALS AND REVIEW. 

Acts for the Commissioners in adjudicating appeals by individuals and agencies from decisions of the central operating offices and regional offices of the Commission regarding matters affecting the rights or interests of Federal employees and arising under laws, rules, or regulations administered by the Commission, including appeals of employees from separations and certain other adverse decisions of appointing officers; appeals from reduction-in-force actions; appeals from ratings in postmaster, rural carrier, and other central-office examinations; appeals from actions taken under the Retirement Act; appeals relative to the suitability of applicants for, and appointees to, positions in the competitive Federal service; and appeals for salary retention, but excluding position-classification appeals and Hatch

Act cases. Also, the Board administers the board-of-review program for deciding performance-rating appeals in the Washington metropolitan area and provides chairmen for such boards. 

OFFICE OF CAREER DEVELOPMENT.- 

Develops, promotes, and carries out nationwide programs to assure effective training, development, and utilization of Federal career employees.

Coordinates and promotes interagency training activities throughout the Federal Government under the provisions of the Government Employees Train ing Act. Assists agencies to assess their training needs and to establish, operate, and evaluate career development and training plans. Assists in the development, establishment, and improvement of non-Government educational programs. Facilitates executive utilization. 

Develops and conducts training in areas included within the functional responsibilities of the Civil Service 

Commission, in areas for which training responsibility has been assigned to the Commission, and in areas of special Federal need. As an integral part of this function, operates the Executive Seminar Center program. 

Fosters and coordinates the Government-wide Incentive Awards Program which encourages exceptional performance by Federal employees through efforts which: provide monetary and honorary awards for superior performance, exceptional achievements, and useful innovations, enhance the attractiveness of the career service by recognition of distinguished work, and improve the image of the Federal employee by publicizing his outstanding accomplishments.

PUBLIC INFORMATION OFFICE.-Fur nishes information to news media regarding personnel needs of the Federal competitive civil service and actions of the Commission affecting Federal personnel management; prepares public-address material and informational pamphlets and articles concerning the Federal civil service; furnishes public speakers to interested

groups; prepares exhibits, audio-visual, and radio-television material connected with recruitment; provides information materials to Federal employees and their organizations; and answers inquiries from news media and the public on civil-service matters. 

OFFICE OF HEARING EXAMINERS. 

Advises the Commission through the Executive Director on all matters relating to hearing examiners and directs a nationwide program for their em ployment and compensation. Main tains close liaison with chief hearing examiners and other key officials in 

Federal agencies, as well as with bar associations and other legal groups; and provides leadership in all matters concerning the hearing examiner program. 

INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS EM- PLOYEES LOYALTY BOARD.-The Board is concerned with inquiries into the loyalty to the Government of the United States of citizens employed, or considered for employment, by international organizations of which the United States is a member, and makes advisory determinations to the international organizations in such cases. [For regulations codified under Interna tional Organizations Employees Loyalty 

Board, see Code of Federal Regulations, Title 5, Chapter V] BUREAUS Bureau of Recruiting and Examining 

Directs the Government-wide recruiting and examining program for staffing all positions in the competitive civil service. Conducts long- and shortrange studies designed to improve the effectiveness of the staffing of the Federal service. Directs the operation of a nationwide program of college relations and recruitment designed to attract well qualified candidates into the Federal service.

Operates through its own offices and boards of examiners the recruiting and examining program for filling positions in Washington, D.C., and certain field positions which are centralized, including postmasters and rural carriers.

Provides program and technical guid ance to regional offices in the operation of their programs for staffing positions throughout the country. Provides central leadership to the agencies in the use of Boards of U.S. Civil Service 

Examiners in filling positions through competitive examinations.

Directs the program for publicizing employment opportunities in the Federal service to insure that all qualified citizens have opportunity to compete. 

Furnishes information to the public about competitive examinations and employment needs. 

Acts on recommendations of agencies for the according of a competitive status noncompetitively to employees under legislation, Executive orders, and civil-service rules and regulations, preaudits agency requests for appointments on the basis of service of former 

Federal employees, and makes determinations of civil-service status in individual cases as requested. 

Acts on nationwide promotion and training agreements. Operates the Sep arated Career Employee Program for positions in the Washington, D.C., metropolitan area, provides a centralized system of rosters of personnel for use by agencies to fill key positions, and operates an Interdepartmental Place ment Program for the Washington,

D.C., metropolitan area. 

Bureau of Personnel Investigations 

Directs the Commission's investigative program, which includes (1) national agency checks and inquiries and limited personal investigations for nonsensitive positions, (2) full field investigations for sensitive positions, (3) investigations on matters relating to enforcement of civil-service laws and rules, and (4) qualifications investigations of applicants for high-level administrative and professional positions.

Formulates plans with respect to the national operation of the Commission's investigative program under DC

public laws and Executive orders.

Develops procedures and negotiates agreements with other investigative agencies to assure effective operations and to facilitate exchange of investigative information. Provides program coordination and maintains liaison with agencies to insure that the Commission's investigations meet their needs for determining fitness and se lecting quality personnel. Advises agencies as to the application of suitability standards. 

Determines workload and controls all full field investigations made by the Commission for other agencies. 

Conducts personal investigations in the metropolitan area of Washington,

D.C. Decides on suitability of ap pointees to nonsensitive competitive positions in the metropolitan area. 

Evaluates all nonsensitive cases under the Commission's jurisdiction when full field loyalty investigation has been conducted by the Federal Bureau of 

Investigation. Considers initial appeals from its own decisions and from suitability decisions by metropolitan area boards of examiners.

Conducts a continuing study of the manner in which the security program established by Executive Order 

10450 of April 27, 1953, is being implemented by the departments and agencies. 

Bureau of Inspections 

The Bureau of Inspections plans, on a nationwide basis, evaluations of personnel management at both departmental and field activities of Government agencies; reviews personnel management practices in Federal agencies within the Washington metropolitan area, including the effectiveness with which management carries out its responsibilities under the Classi fication Act of 1949. 

It also evaluates the effectiveness of agency personnel management in terms of its contribution to the accomplishment of agency mission and the degree to which it accords with public policy and individual employee rights established by other laws or regulation; where necessary, assists agencies in improving their management of people; makes recommendations to bring about adherence to established policies, standards, and practices; serves as a clearinghouse for the exchange of information among agencies on the most efficient and economical personnel management policies, procedures, and practices; maintains liaison with agency headquarters offices and advises on specific problems as requested.

Develops procedures and technical instructions for field and departmental inspection staff, and furnishes technical advice on classification matters to regional offices; acts on requests of employees and agencies to classify specific positions; acts on appeals under the Classification Act of 1949 

and under the Postal Field Serv ice Compensation Act of 1955; and reviews and recommends action on requests to place positions in grades 

GS-16, 17, and 18.

OFFICE SERVICES DIVISION.-IS re sponsible for: (1) office space, including space acquisition, use, maintenance, and improvement; procurement, storage, control, and distribution of supplies, furniture, and equipment; and management of transportation and communication facilities; (2) publication management, including composition, proofreading, art-graphics, printing, binding, and distribution of issuances; (3) records management, including all related procedures, as preservation, retirement, disposition, surveys, and systems; central files; receiving and dispatching mail; and (4) developing and coordinating emergency communications and facilities. 

LIBRARY.-Maintains a specialized collection of current and historical materials on all phases of public and personnel administration. Performs extensive research and reference work in civil service and related fields and compiles bibliographies on subjects of interest to personnel administrators. 

PERSONNEL DIVISION.-This division is responsible for the planning, administration, and implementation of an internal personnel program creatively identified with the Commission's Government-wide personnel management goals. The internal personnel program, operating as an integral part of overall Commission management, is designed to help management accomplish its mission through the acquisition, development, and effective utilization of employees.

Bureau of Programs and Standards The Bureau of Programs and Stand ards is responsible for a coordinated program of policy development, planning, and standards setting in the areas of Federal personnel administration with which the Civil Service Commission is concerned. 

PROGRAM PLANNING DIVISION.-Is responsible for conducting studies, developing plans, and recommending policies and programs to improve and strengthen Federal personnel management. Prepares the Commission's legislative program, the annual report of the Commission, and the annual training report; advises congressional and executive officials in regard to Federal personnel management; and provides leadership in installing new programs.

Areas covered include employee benefits and services, employment policies and systems, training programs, employee-management relations and cooperation, manpower policies and management of the Federal personnel system in a national emergency, overseas personnel management, scientific and engineering personnel programs, pay administration, and position classification. 

PROGRAM SYSTEMS AND INSTRUC- TIONS DIVISION.-Develops implement ing policies and procedures, and prepares and interprets regulations and instructions for agency guidance in carrying out laws, programs, and legal decisions. Areas covered include the fields of personnel recruitment, examining, and selection; pay and leave systems; conferring competitive status; requirements for employment; grievance and appeals systems; and in such other programs as ing, promotion, demotion, removal, suspension, and reduction in force.

Develops and administers the system for issuing personnel instructions. Develops procedures for, coordinates, and evaluates the operations of the overall

Commission appeals program at the train-

first appellate level and provides technical advisory service to agencies.

STANDARDS DIVISION.-Establishes and issues classification standards for the approximately 1,000,000 positions paid under the Classification Act of 

1949. Establishes and issues qualifica tion standards for approximately 

2,000,000 positions filled under the merit system established by the Civil 

Service Act of 1883. Devises tests and other methods for measuring qualifications for original appointment and for transfer, promotion, and other personnel actions. Performs related ocscupational studies and personnel measurement research.

Regional Offices 

The Commission maintains 10 regional offices located in principal cities throughout the country. Service throughout geographic areas covered is provided by the regional offices through a network of 50 civil service representatives, and more than 100 

other duty stations. Regional offices. 

also have jurisdiction over some 1,000 examining points located in the larger post offices, and about 750 Boards of 

U.S. Civil Service Examiners located at Federal establishments to conduct recruiting and examining for those agencies under merit procedures. 

Each regional office coordinates and directs the Federal Government's recruitment program designed to attract the highest quality applicants from among the Nation's school and college graduates and the general public; disseminates information on civil service examinations and Federal employment matters; conducts and rates examinations, furnishes lists of eligibles to appointing officials, and supervises similar activities carried out by the boards of examiners; conducts qualifications, security, and other personnel investigations and determines the suitability of applicants for Federal employment; coordinates training and career development efforts on an interagency basis to secure maximum utilization of training resources; inspects personnel operations and evaluates personnel management programs of agency field installations; furnishes personnel management consultative and advisory

515 service to Federal establishments, administers the Commission's medical, handicapped, and veteran programs and maintains liaison with schools, colleges, unions, public, and private veterans' organizations, and other groups having an interest in Federal employment matters; adjudicates appeals involving suspension, discharge, furlough, reduction in rank or compensation, reduction-in-force, salary retention, and position classification; and performs other work essential to the administration of the Federal civil service.

Regulations, Title 22, Chapter V; Title 41, Chapter 19] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

United States Information Agency was established by Reorganization Plan 8 

of 1953, effective August 1, 1953, to carry out international information activities as authorized by the United 

States Information and Educational 

Exchange Act of 1948, as amended (62 

Stat. 6; 22 U.S.C. 1431). The inter national educational and cultural activities of the Agency are authorized by the United States Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 (75 Stat. 527; 22 U.S.C. 2451). 

Other basic statutory and executive authorities affecting the organization and activities of the Agency are:

the act of August 9, 1939 (53 Stat. 1290; 

22 U.S.C. 501, 502); Foreign Service

Act of 1946, as amended (60 Stat. 999; 

22 U.S.C. 801 note); India Emergency Food Aid Act of 1951 (65 Stat. 70; 

50 U.S.C. 2311 note) under delegations made by the Department of State, April 12-15, 1954; and Executive Orders 10477 of August 1, 1953, as amended by 10822 of May 20, 1959, 10522 of March 26, 1954, and 10900 

of January 5, 1961; Executive Orders 

10973 of November 3, 1961, and 11034 of June 25, 1962.

PURPOSE.-The purpose of the

United States Information Agency is to help achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives by influencing public attitudes in other nations, and advising the President, his representatives abroad, and the various departments and agencies on the implications of foreign opinion for present and contemplated U.S. policies, programs, and official statements. This purpose is carried out by using personal contact, radio broadcasting, libraries, book publication and distribution, press, motion pictures, television, exhibits, Englishlanguage instruction, and other means of communication to encourage constructive public support abroad for U.S. policy objectives, and to unmask and counter hostile attempts to distort or frustrate the objectives and policies of the United States. While the Director of the United States Information Agency takes the initiative in offering counsel, the various departments and agencies seek such counsel when considering policies and programs which may substantially affect or be affected by foreign opinion.

ROPE).-Each Assistant Director for an area is responsible for the direction, coordination, and management of the 

United States information programs for the countries of his assigned geographic area. They supply a knowledge of field problems and requirements to the Agency's policy and planning processes. They arrange with media services for the provision of media products to their areas. They consult with appropriate area and country officers in the 

Department of State, the Agency for 

International Development, and with other agencies, on operational matters of mutual concern.

OFFICE OF POLICY.-This office for mulates basic information policies, themes, and program emphases for the Agency. It obtains policy and background information from the Department of State and other sources and prepares policy guidance for operating elements of the Agency. It coordinates media output so that the content will accurately reflect Agency policy and emphasis. Members of the Office main tain liaison with the White House, De partments of State and Defense, and other agencies, and represent the 

Agency on interdepartmental groups concerned with foreign affairs. The Of fice has on its staff specialists in national security, science, space, economics, youth and students, cultural affairs, labor, minorities, and women's activities. A staff member serves as the 

Agency Representative at the U.S. 

Mission to the United Nations and advises the U.S. Mission on foreign public opinion factors in U.S. policies and actions in the United Nations. The

Foreign Correspondents Center in New 

York, under the supervision of the Office of Policy, provides assistance to foreign correspondents reporting on and interpreting America and its policies to their home countries.

OFFICE OF THE GENERAL COUNSEL.- 

This office advises the Agency on the meaning and intent of all laws, regulations, and Executive orders which authorize the Agency's programs or relate to their authorities and limitations thereon. This office also assists in the drafting of proposed legislation, Executive order proposals, regulations, contracts, and leases. The General 

Counsel also supplements the personal relations of the Director with the Congress.

OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATION.-This office develops, interprets, and applies administrative and management policies and procedures necessary to assure effective operation of the Agency's programs. It provides central management, budget, fiscal, contract and procurement, and administrative services for the Agency.

MEDIA SERVICES.-The Broadcasting 

Service produces and broadcasts radio programs in English and foreign languages, including the operation of broadcasting and relay facilities to transmit these programs. It also furnishes technical direction to the Agency's field offices in the utilization of radio program materials broadcast through indigenous outlets and supplies packaged programs to these offices for such use. Broadcasting activities are devoted primarily to countries within the Soviet Orbit and, secondarily, to selected areas of the Free World. 

The Information Center Service furnishes technical direction and assistance to information centers, libraries, and binational cultural centers. It promotes the distribution of American books, both English and local languages, to individuals and institutions of particular local significance. This service also prepares exhibits reflecting 

American culture and achievement, and materials for a program for training local teachers of English. It also conducts the Informational Media 

Guaranty Program.

The Motion Picture Service con tracts for the production of, or otherwise acquires, motion pictures in appropriate languages for use abroad through commercial outlets or for

showings conducted by USIS posts.

It furnishes USIS posts with equipment and supplies necessary to conduct such showings, and provides technical direction on the use of such materials and equipment.

The Press and Publications Service produces or acquires and furnishes press materials, pamphlets, magazines, and photo services to the USIS posts overseas and provides technical direction on the utilization of such products. 

The Television Service produces or acquires the television films and tapes for use by local television stations and networks in overseas countries through 

USIS posts and provides technical direction and advice on the effective employment of the television medium. 

OFFICE OF PERSONNEL AND TRAIN- 

ING. This office plans and executes personnel programs, including recruitment, examination, selection, and placement of employees, career development, and position classification; and plans and conducts orientation and training programs for domestic and foreign service employees.

OFFICE OF PRIVATE COOPERATION.- 

This office is responsible for obtaining the fullest possible use of the contributed services and facilities of nongovernmental agencies to further the objectives of the information program. 

OFFICE OF PUBLIC INFORMATION.- The Office of Public Information is re sponsible for the Agency's reporting on its programs to the American public. 

The Office serves as point of contact within the Agency for newspapers, radio, television, and general public requests for information.

RESEARCH AND REFERENCE SERV- 

ICE. This office prepares data on psychological factors and propaganda problems which must be considered in formulating information policies. It furnishes research data which will aid in the planning and execution of media service programs. It also furnishes information about significant trends in operations and about program accom plishments. 

OFFICE OF SECURITY.-This office is responsible for personnel, physical, and documentary security. It also serves as the investigative arm of the Agency.

FIELD OPERATIONS.-Agency offices abroad, known as the United States.

Information Service, under the supervision of the Chiefs of Mission, conduct public information, public relations and cultural activities-i.e., those activities intended to inform or influence foreign public opinion-for agencies of the U.S. Government except for Commands of the Department of Defense. Each USIS office is headed by a Public Affairs Officer who is a member of the "country team" under the Chief of the United States Diplomatic Mission.

Regulations, Title 19, Chapter II] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

United States Tariff Commission was created by act of Congress approved 

September 8, 1916 (39 Stat. 795).

The Commission's present powers and duties are provided for largely by the 

Tariff Act of June 17, 1930 (title III, part II, 46 Stat. 696; 19 U.S.C. 1330 

et seq.); the Antidumping Act, 1921, as amended; the Agricultural Adjustment Act, as amended; and Executive 

Orders 11075 of January 15, 1963, and 

11106 of April 18, 1963.

PURPOSE. It is the primary duty of the Commission to investigate and report upon tariff and foreign trade matters, as required by statute. It makes such investigations and reports at the request of the President, either branch of the Congress, the House Committee on Ways and Means, or the Senate 

Committee on Finance. Investigations into the effects on domestic industries, firms, or groups of workers, of increased imports resulting from trade agreements concessions may be initiated by the interested parties. The 

Commission also makes studies, surveys, or investigations on its own initiative.

ORGANIZATION.-The Commission consists of six members, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate for terms of 6 years, one term expiring each year. Not more than three commissioners may be of the same political party. The President is authorized to designate the Chairman and Vice Chairman annually from the membership of the Commission. The Staff Coordinating Committee, composed of senior officers of the Commission's staff and chaired by the 

Chief of the Economics Division, plans and supervises the substantive work of the Commission under the active direction of the Commission. The operating divisions of the staff consist of the office of the General Counsel; the office of the Director of Investigation; the Economics Division; and, under the direction of the Chief, Technical 

Services, seven commodity divisions, the Accounting Division, the Statis tical Division, and an Invoice Analysis 

Section. The Office of the Secretary acts as the secretariat for the Commission, is charged with the conduct of relations with the public and other Government agencies, and issues publications and notices. Personnel, budget activities, and general administrative and auxiliary services are under the 

Director of Administration.

UNITED STATES TARIFF COMMISSION 

521 

ACTIVITIES The Commission conducts a variety of public investigations which usually involve a public notice, public hearing, and a formal report. It also undertakes research activities and studies relating to commercial and customs policy. 

PUBLIC INVESTIGATIONS. Trade Agreements program.-Section 221 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 (76 

Stat. 874; 19 U.S.C. 1841) requires the

Commission, with respect to each article that may be considered for a trade agreement concession, to advise the President of its judgment as to the probable economic effect of a reduction in the import duty or other import restriction on the industries producing like or directly competitive articles. 

Section 301 of that act requires the

Commission to conduct investigations upon petition on behalf of an industry, a firm, or a group of workers, to determine whether, as a result in major part of trade agreement concessions, an article is being imported in such increased quantities as to constitute the major cause or threat of serious injury to the petitioning industry or firm, or unemployment or underemployment of a significant number or proportion of workers of a firm or appropriate subdivision thereof. Industry investigations must be completed, and a report made to the 

President, within 6 months; investigations of petitions by firms or workers must be completed, and a report made to the President, within 60 days.

Section 351 (d) of the act (76 Stat. 

899; 19 U.S.C. 1981) requires the Tariff Commission to report annually with respect to developments within an industry that has been granted tariff relief and, after formal investigation on its own motion or on request of the 

President, to advise the President of the probable economic effect of the reduction or elimination of the tariff increase that has been granted.

Sections 402 and 403 of the act (76 

Stat. 902; 19 U.S.C. 1803, 1804) directs the Commission to submit an 743-116°-65-34 annual report to the Congress on the operation of the trade agreements program and to keep advised at all times of the effects of trade agreements entered into under the program.

Dumping investigations.-Section 

201(a) of the Antidumping Act, 1921 (19 U.S.C. 160), provides that whenever the Secretary of the Treasury determines that a class or kind of merchandise is being, or is likely to be, sold in the United States at less than its fair value, the Tariff Commission is directed to determine within 3 months whether a domestic industry is being or is likely to be injured, or is prevented from being established, as a result of such importations and to notify the 

Secretary of the Treasury of its determination.

Import interference with agricul tural programs.-Section 22 of the Ag ricultural Adjustment Act, as amended 

(7 U.S.C. 624), requires the Tariff 

Commission, on direction of the President, to conduct an immediate investigation to determine whether any articles are being or are practically certain to be imported into the United

States under such conditions and in such quantities as to materially interfere with programs of the Department of Agriculture for agricultural commodities or products thereof, or to reduce substantially the amount of any product processed in the United States from such commodities or products. 

On the basis of the Commission's investigation and report to the President of its findings and recommendation, the President is authorized to restrict the imports in question by imposition of either import fees or quotas.

Investigations pursuant to specific re quests of the President or of the Congress.-Section 332 of the Tariff Act of 

1930 (19 U.S.C. 1332), directs the

Commission to make such investigations and reports as may be requested by the President, the House Committee on Ways and Means, the Senate Com mittee on Finance, or by either branch of the Congress. Public investigations

undertaken under this section arise chiefly from congressional resolutions involving formal investigations regarding specific products or industries. 

Tariff schedules and classification. 

Under section 332 of the Tariff Act of 

1930, the Commission is also directed to investigate the relationship between the rates of duty on raw materials and finished or partly finished products, the effects of duties, and questions relative to the arrangement of tariff schedules and the classification of articles therein. 

Section 201 of the Tariff Classification 

Act of 1962 authorizes the Commission to issue, at appropriate intervals, and to keep up to date a publication containing current tariff schedules and related matters, including such matters as may be needed for reporting statistics. Section 484 (e) of the Tar iff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1484) directs the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Commerce, and the

Chairman of the Tariff Commission to establish statistical procedures for the enumeration of imports. 

Differences in costs of foreign and domestic production.-Section 336 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 

1336), the so-called flexible tariff provision, sets forth the procedure by which the import duty on commodities may be changed by proclamation of the President after investigation and report by the Commission regarding differences in the costs of production in the United States and the principal competing foreign country. The provisions of this section apply only to articles on which a tariff concession is not in effect pursuant to a trade agreement. 

Unfair practices in import trade.

Under section 337 of the Tariff Act of 

1930, as amended (19 U.S.C. 1337), the Tariff Commission is authorized to conduct investigations regarding allegations that unfair methods of competition or unfair acts are being committed in the importation of articles into the United States, or in their domestic sale, the effect or tendency of which is to substantially injure or destroy an efficiently and economically operated domestic industry. Where such methods or acts are found to exist, the Commission reports to the President, who may direct that the articles involved be excluded from entry into the United States. 

COMMERCIAL AND CUSTOMS POL- ICY. Under various sections of the 

Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, and other legislation, the Commission conducts analytical studies pertinent to trade and tariff policy; develops information on tariff relations between the United States and foreign countries and on commercial policies and prac tices of foreign countries; and is continuously engaged in the collection of a wide range of technical and economic data relating to the economic conditions underlying competition between domestic and foreign industries. 

Under section 332 of the act, the Commission is directed to place such information at the disposal of the 

President and the Congress whenever requested, and on its own motion it periodically publishes special reports or studies relating to such matters. Section 334 of the 1930 act (19 U.S.C. 

1334) directs the Commission to cooperate with, and furnish technical and other information to, other Government agencies in appropriate matters. Under this and other provisions of law the Commission works closely with a number of other Government agencies, particularly in compiling information required in the conduct of the U.S. trade agreements program. 

Section 338 of the act (19 U.S.C. 

1338) authorizes the Commission to investigate discrimination against the foreign commerce of the United States and authorizes the President to impose discriminatory duties on the products of a foreign country which is found to be discriminating against the commerce of the United States.

Approved. 

BEN DORFMAN, Chairman.

[For regulations codified under Veterans Administration, see Code of 

Federal Regulations, Title 38, Chapter I; Title 41, Chapter 8] CREATION AND AUTHORITY.-The 

Veterans Administration was established as an independent agency under the President by Executive Order 5398, of July 21, 1930, in accordance with the act of July 3, 1930 (46 Stat. 

1016). This act authorized the President to consolidate and coordinate 

Federal agencies especially created for or concerned in the administration of laws providing benefits for veterans.

PURPOSE.- -The Veterans Admin istration administers laws authorizing benefits for former members of the Armed Forces and for the dependents and other beneficiaries of deceased former members of such forces. The 

Veterans Administration benefits avail able under various acts of Congress include: compensation for serviceconnected disability or death; pension for non-service-connected disability or death; dependency and indemnity compensation; vocational rehabilitation for service-connected disability; education and training; war orphans' educational assistance; guaranty or insurance of home, farm, and business loans, and, under certain conditions, direct home loans; United States

Government and National Service Life 

Insurance; insurance indemnity; hospitalization; domiciliary care; outpatient medical and dental care for service-connected disability; prosthetic and other appliances; special housing for certain seriously disabled veterans; automobiles or other conveyances for certain disabled veterans; World War 

I adjusted service certificates; a guardianship program for the protection of estates derived from Veterans Administration benefits paid to incompetent or minor beneficiaries; burial allowances; and burial flags. In addition the Veterans Administration admin isters the insurance section of the Sol diers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act for persons in the active military service.

ORGANIZATION.-The Veterans Ad ministration is under the charge of the Administrator of Veterans Affairs, who is responsible for the administration of all laws governing the Vet erans Administration. 

The Veterans Administration is organizationally divided as follows: 

1. The Central Office.-The central office of the Veterans Administration consists of the following staff offices and departments, the heads of which are directly responsible to the Administrator of Veterans Affairs for the proper performance of all the functions assigned to them: 

STAFF OFFICES Office of the Director, Information Service. 

Office of the Controller.

Management and Evaluation.

Department of Data Management. 

Department of Veterans Benefits. 

2. The Field Stations. This term applies to Veterans Administration installations located in the field, and includes the following:

Insurance Centers. 

Regional offices. 

Veterans Benefits Office (D. C.). 

Hospitals. 

Centers. 

Outpatient Clinics. 

Domiciliaries. 

VA offices. 

Supply depots.

Data processing centers. 

CENTRAL OFFICE ACTIVITIES Office of the Administrator 

The Administrator is responsible to the President for the administration of veterans affairs and the laws which govern them. He is directly responsible for the establishment of the basic policies governing agency operation; the development and maintenance of its basic organization structure; the interpretation of laws pertaining to veterans affairs, and the establishment of supplementary regulations; the stimu lation and approval of long-range plans; and the development and maintenance of favorable relations with important organizations, groups, and individuals interested in veterans affairs. The Administrator serves as the adviser to the President on veterans affairs.

VETERANS ADMINISTRATION 

527 

Office of the Deputy Administrator 

The Deputy Administrator is the principal assistant to the Administrator in the overall administration of the 

Veterans Administration. He takes independent action for the Administrator on all problems affecting the VA which do not require the Administrator's personal attention and acts for the 

Administrator in the latter's absence. 

Office of the Associate Deputy

Administrator 

The Associate Deputy Administrator assists the Administrator and the Deputy Administrator in the administration of the following staff activities: office methods and administration, -supply management, budget, construction, safety and fire protection, fiscal, personnel, management audits, investigations, emergency preparedness planning, and security. He takes independent action for the Administrator on all problems in these activities which do not require the personal attention of the Administrator or the 

Deputy Administrator. He acts for the 

Deputy Administrator in the latter's absence and for the Administrator in the absence of both the Administrator and the Deputy Administrator. 2203 

Office of the Assistant Deputy

Administrator 

The Assistant Deputy Administra tor, as full assistant to the Administrator and the Deputy Administrator, participates in high-level policy discussions and contributes recommendations regarding solutions of problems and decisions to be made on all programs administered by the Veterans Administration. As directed, he represents the Administrator with the Congress, other Federal agencies, and the Bureau of the Budget. He also acts for the 

Associate Deputy Administrator in the latter's absence and for the Deputy Administrator in the absence of both the Deputy Administrator and the Associate Deputy Administrator. He makes independent recommendations to the Administrator as to areas which should receive priority in substantive research and recommends approval, disapproval, or revision of plans submitted by department heads and staff officers. He is the Administrator's top planning officer and director of substantive research. 

Office of the Executive Assistant 

This office, the central coordinating staff for the Office of the Administrator, presents matters to the Administrator requiring his personal attention, monitors special projects and assignments, and insures that required action is controlled and coordinated. It acts as point of contact for operating matters coming to the Office of the Administrator and is responsible for the last line of review before an action is taken or a decision is made in the operations of the VA. It makes inquiries into operating matters of interest; evaluates proposals for changes in operating policies and recommends approval, disapproval, further study or other appropriate action; coordinates proposals with operating officials to assure their presentation is in the form desired; and follows up to assure that decisions once made are implemented. Discharges for the Administrator all matters of an administrative nature within the Office. 

Administrator's Advisory Council

The Chairman advises the Adminis trator on long-range policies, plans, research programs, organization, and whether established programs are meeting these objectives. The Council is concerned with such matters as how veterans compare with nonveterans, what are the handicaps and needs of veterans in various categories, what new programs are needed, what changes to established programs should be made, and the long-range impact of both existing and proposed programs

upon sociological and economic welfare of the veteran population as a whole.

Contract Appeals Board 

This board, under a Chairman, represents the Administrator in ascertaining the facts and circumstances attending appeals by contractors from decisions of Veterans Administration contracting officers under construction, architect-engineer, and supply contracts and renders final decisions on such appeals.

Board of Veterans Appeals The Board of Veterans Appeals, under a Chairman and Vice Chairman, has statutory jurisdiction to decide appeals to the Administrator for benefits under all laws administered by the 

Veterans Administration (38 U.S.C. 

4001-4009). Its decisions are final, except as to issues on insurance contracts which are subject to action in the Federal district courts.

STAFF OFFICES Office of the Director, Information Service The Office of the Director, Infor mation Service, formulates basic policies governing Veterans Administration public information programs; counsels and advises the Administrator and other levels of management where public interest is involved in the deter mination of Veterans Administration policy; reviews and coordinates programs for informing the public of Veterans Administration activities in areas of special interest to operating departments; and keeps informed of and appraises for the Administrator the results of public information programs. 

This office develops and maintains relationships with national information outlets and contacts; and obtains, assembles, prepares, and coordinates information for release through press, radio, and other media to advise veterans and dependents on benefits ad ministered by the Veterans Admin istration and to provide information concerning the offices where applications for benefits may be made. 

Office of the Controller 

The Controller is the top financial management officer of the Veterans 

Administration. He is responsible to the Administrator for the economical and efficient use of all funds available to the agency and for the control, direction, and administration of all fi nancial operations. He is responsible for reports management and the basic reports structure of the agency, and in research statistics he provides staff support and publications on the veteran population, its characteristics, composition, and participation in Veterans Administration programs. In addition, he is the principal representative of the Veterans Administration on budg et, appropriations, accounting, financial auditing, and other fiscal matters with the Bureau of the Budget, the 

Congress, the Treasury Department, the General Accounting Office, and other Government agencies.

The Controller's office includes a Budget Service, Financial Management Service, Reports Management Service, and Research Statistics Serv ice, in addition to his immediate office. 

These Services operate in their functional areas VA-wide to assist the Controller in discharging his responsibilities.

Office of the General Counsel The General Counsel serves as chief law officer of the Veterans Administration in all matters of law and legislation. He is responsible to the 

Administrator for the interpretation of all laws affecting veterans or their

VETERANS ADMINISTRATION 

529 dependents and for establishing precedent decisions of the Administrator based upon such laws. 

This office renders legal advice and other legal services to all department heads and top staff officers and assists in the formulation of governing regulations and amendments thereto, reviewing for legal correctness all such regulations or directives; it collaborates with the Department of Justice in the handling of all litigation arising from 

Veterans Administration programs or operations or involving the Veterans

Administration or any official thereof and, in conjunction with or by agreement with the Department of Justice, may handle certain types of litigation is in State or Federal courts.

This office handles all matters pertaining to proposed legislation, Execuorders tive and proclamations, affecting the Veterans Administration, except appropriations, including the preparation of all reports concerning such matters to committees of Congress, the President, the Bureau of the 

Budget, and other executive agencies; represents the Administrator in congressional committees and other hearings and interdepartmental conferences on legislative matters.

This office maintains liaison with the Senate and House committees and contact activities in both Houses of Congress. 

Office of the Assistant Administrator for Management and Evaluation 

This office evaluates VA operations through management audits, investigations, and manpower utilization analyses. It has staff responsibility for VA's personnel and document security, purchasing and supply, emergency planning coordination, nondiscrimination in employment and VA contracts, and work improvement and paperwork management programs. It evaluates 

VA's internal appraisal mechanisms. It recommends policies and provides staff guidance to the Administrator and top 

VA officials on these matters. 

Office of the Assistant Administrator for Construction 

The Assistant Administrator for

Construction develops general policies and plans of VA-wide application for: (1) design, construction, and preservation of VA hospitals, domiciliaries, and other buildings; (2) real property management, including acquisition, economical utilization, protection, and disposal of real property and interests therein; and (3) accident and fire prevention, fire protection, and disaster relief planning. This office controls design and construction of hospitals, domiciliaries, and other facilities, major alterations, and improvements. 

It acquires real property and property interests in fee and disposes of such real property and interests where excess to the needs of the Veterans Administration (not including transactions within the veterans loan guaranty program). 

Office of the Assistant Administrator for Personnel

The Office of Personnel advises and assists the Administrator in all matters relating to personnel administration in the Veterans Administration. It plans, formulates, and recommends agencywide personnel policies, programs, and practices. It also has responsibility for administering the central office personnel program. It serves as the principal representative of the Veterans Administration with the Civil Service

Commission, employee organizations, and other groups on personnel management matters. 

Office of the Manager,

Administrative Services The Manager, Administrative Serv ices, under the Associate Deputy Administrator, furnishes VA-wide services

in the areas of claimant identification and folder location, records development, language translation, visual aids, printing, reproduction, and distribution. 

For Central Office elements, he provides office services support, including fiscal and supply services, space allocation, building maintenance and liaison with General Services Administration, and safety and fire protection. He serves as principal representative of the VA with other organi zations on matters pertaining to all these Central Office services support activities.

Department of Medicine and Surgery improvement, and work simplification 

The Chief Medical Director is re sponsible for the proper conduct of the activities of the Department of 

Medicine and Surgery and insures complete medical and hospital service for the medical care and treatment of veterans, as prescribed by the Administrator of Veterans Affairs pursuant to 38 U.S.C. 4101-4115 and other statutory authority and regulations. 

The Deputy Chief Medical Director serves as principal assistant to the Chief Medical Director in the discharge of his responsibilities, and acts for the Chief Medical Director in the latter's absence.

The Associate Deputy Chief Med ical Director assists the above officials and coordinates the activities of the administrative elements of the Department.

OFFICE OF ASSISTANT CHIEF MEDICAL DIRECTOR FOR MANAGEMENT AND EVAL- UATION.-Develops policies and plans and coordinates development of criteria for audits, surveys, and evaluations of field station management and operations; coordinates internal and external evaluation inspection activities; audits and evaluates performance of Central Office departmental activ ities; evaluates overall effectiveness of audits and surveys and the application of management controls, and recommends action for correction of deficiencies or to accomplish improvements; and coordinates the conduct of systematic review, productivity measurement, manpower utilization, management programs. Reviews proposed legisla tion and Executive orders to determine effect upon the medical program and makes recommendations thereon; recommends changes to existing laws affecting medical benefits; and advises on legal matters and collaborates with the Office of the General Counsel on matters relating to the legal and legislative aspects of the medical program. 

Processes all inquiries from outside sources relating to applicants for, or recipients of, the medical benefits of the VA; takes action on all complaint and complimentary mail; and is responsible for action on reports on emergency situations at field stations.

Reviews and takes action on all investigations.

Department of Veterans Benefits The Chief Benefits Director con ducts the activities of the Department of Veterans Benefits. He insures the effective execution of an integrated program of veterans benefits consisting of compensation and pension, vocational rehabilitation and education, loan guaranty, guardianship, and contact activities of the Veterans Administration.

The Deputy Chief Benefits Director serves as the full assistant to the Chief 

Benefits Director in the discharge of his responsibilities and acts for him in his absence. 

OFFICE OF THE DIRECTOR, EVALUA- TION STAFF. This office (1) develops policies and plans for processing and utilization of all data relating to effectiveness of field stations and Central 

Office, DVB activities; (2) evaluates overall department effectiveness in applying management control, reporting, inspection, measurement, and evaluation techniques; (3) audits and evaluates performance of Central Office, DVB staff and line elements; and (4) performs special assignments as di rected by the Chief Benefits Director. 

OFFICE OF THE DIRECTOR, COMPEN- SATION, PENSION AND EDUCATION SERVICE. Formulates plans, policies, regulations, procedures, and standards of departmentwide application, pertaining to disability compensation and pension claims; claims for automobiles or other conveyances; special housing claims; eligibility determinations for other services or Government agencies; death compensation and pension claims; dependency and indemnity compensation; claims for reimbursement for burial, funeral, and transportation expenses of deceased veterans; claims for accrued compensation, pension, dependency and indemnity compensation, retirement pay; waivers of overpayments (other than loan guaranty); forfeiture of rights and benefits; claims for Government insurance by beneficiaries of deceased veterans; claims for servicemen's indemnity; and claims for adjusted compensation in death cases; claims for vocational rehabilitation of disabled veterans, and educational assistance and special restorative training for children of service-connected totally disabled veterans, or children of veterans who died of a disease or injury incurred or aggravated in active service in the Armed Forces during wartime or during the induction period under Selective Service. 

Reviews proposed legislation and

Executive orders pertaining to the compensation, pension, vocational rehabilitation and education programs and comments and recommends with respect thereto. It appraises the effectiveness, efficiency and economy of policies, regulations, procedures and standards in implementing public laws and obtaining program objectives; formulates performance standards for the compensation, pension, and education program; and prepares and readjusts the Schedule for Rating Dis abilities and formulates administrative issues and rating decisions as concom itants thereof. Maintains top level cooperative working relations with other Federal agencies and national organizations and associations which deal with or have an interest in the compensation, pension, and educational benefits administered by this office.

OFFICE OF THE DIRECTOR, LOAN GUARANTY SERVICE.-Formulates poli cies, plans, procedures, and standards of departmentwide application pertaining to programs whereby Veterans Administration effectuates the provisions of 38 U.S.C. Ch. 37 and other statutes and implementing Executive orders and comparable directives relating to direct and indirect

Government financial assistance for the purchase or construction of homes, and the acquisition, management, and operation of business and farming enterprises by veterans, and related activities consequent upon the default, sale, or other disposition of the veterans' contractual obligations and properties. 

Advises as to approved precedent interpretations of laws and regulations and the application of policies and procedures on loan guaranty programs, and prepares decisions in relation thereto. Directs a program of financial research and the continuous analysis and evaluation of economic data and trends affecting residential, business, and farm financing. Furnishes legal advice to all elements of the Department pertaining to the guaranty, insurance, and making of loans and directs action on all appeals received from lenders and builders suspended from the program. 

This office reviews proposed legislation and Executive orders pertaining to loan guaranty programs and recommends thereon. Recommends proposals for consideration of changes in existing laws relating to loan guaranty programs. Maintains top level liaison with other components of Federal

Government and other organizations and associations interested in the loan guaranty program.

OFFICE OF THE DIRECTOR, INSURANCE SERVICE.-Formulates plans, regula tions, procedures, and standards at servicewide application pertaining to adjudication of disability insurance claims involving waiver of premiums and payment of disability insurance awards; authorization of policy loans, cash surrenders, and matured endowments; billing, collecting (excluding the receipt and deposit of payments), and crediting payments for insurance premiums, loans and liens. Conducts allotment transactions with the service departments and payroll transactions with commercial employers. Determines whether death or disability is directly traceable to the extra hazards of military or naval service and authorizes transfer from appropriation to funds. 

Conducts transactions with commercial insurers for guarantee of premium payments under Article IV of the Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act of 

1940, as amended; conducts studies of mortality and disability to calculate and establish policy rates and values, determines surplus and apportionment of dividends, and compiles actuarial statements. Appraises the effectiveness, efficiency, and economy of policies, regulations, procedures, and standards in implementing public laws and obtaining program objectives and the significant effect of the insurance program nationally. 

Reviews proposed legislation and

Executive orders to determine the specific effect upon the program and comments and recommends with respect thereto; also recommends changes to existing laws affecting the insurance program. Participates in congressional hearings on proposed legislation, when required. Maintains liaison with agencies, organizations, and commercial activities interested in life insurance.

Recommends with respect to allotments to be made from funds under control of the Department and allots funds within overall approved budgetary programs of the Department; and maintains departmentwide accounting and budgetary control records. Formulates and maintains work rate and quality performance standards and related work measurement reporting systems for finance activities.
